We've found HOVERAir drones very easy to use. Once connected to the app, you simply select your preferred flight mode and distance, launch the drone and start riding.

The different flight modes offer plenty of options, too. Dolly Track allows the drone to fly backwards while keeping you in frame, while Follow Me mode tracks your movements automatically.

Tracking performance is impressive, with the X1 ProMax capable of following riders through woodland and keeping up with faster efforts. It can track at speeds of up to 42km/h, with short bursts of up to 60km/h.

When you're finished, simply hold out your hand and the drone will return and land in your palm. Weighing just 192g, it can then be folded away and slipped into a jersey pocket, so there's no need to carry any extra luggage.

The price mentioned here is for the standard HOVERAir X1 ProMax package, but there are also discounts available on several bundles through the HOVERAir website, which include additional accessories to help you get more out of the drone.

If you're interested in trying out a self-flying camera but don't want to spend quite as much, the older HOVERAir X1 is also worth considering. As the predecessor to the PROMAX, it doesn't offer the same 8K capabilities, but it retains the convenient follow-me functionality in a similarly compact design. It's currently 15% off, down to £228.

items.title: Our verdict on Marc Marquez's bombshell MotoGP retirement
items.author: The Race Team
items.content:
Marc Marquez dropped a huge bombshell as the final MotoGP round of the season kicked off at Valencia by announcing he is retiring from racing after this weekend.

Here's our take on the decision.

Who can blame him? Going out on top

There have been suggestions for weeks that Marc would retire at the end of the season, but it’s absolutely worth stressing this: almost none of them have come from inside the MotoGP paddock, with nearly everyone that you speak to (including people very much inside the Marquez inner circle) almost certain that he would continue on.

There was, so went the belief, still so much to come. New regulations for next year, and the chance to do what he’s never done and win on a different spec of bike. The opportunity to give us the moment Casey Stoner denied us, and test himself against his hotshot new Ducati team-mate Pedro Acosta.

Instead, he’s walked away - and honestly, after countless surgeries, dozens of broken bones, and 10 world titles, who can blame him? He’s going out on top, on his own terms.

What it says about his 2026 title

My apologies for bringing Formula 1 into this - I will keep it short. I remember being a fresh-faced editorial assistant when Nico Rosberg dropped his retirement announcement on us in 2016, and while those memories are so incredibly distinct (at home versus on track, new to the industry versus much more settled), the vision of it all is surprisingly similar.

When Rosberg got his one F1 title over the line, it was knife-edge. We all knew - he probably knew, too - that this was the one and only. He clearly accepted that quickly and was happy to leave it at that.

Marquez has won eight in MotoGP, but this is the first one he's won in this way. This is the first one that felt truly knife-edge, that felt lost and then found, that felt like it was taking more out of him than ever before and something different out of him than before.

He points-raced to it, with just a handful of crashes from his return at Mugello six months ago to now, whereas normally he was the one leading the crash standings. This time he played the odds and the opponent, and had to convince his body - the much-suffering arm, the diminished shoulder - to play along.

I have little doubt he could have won again. But I genuinely believe he no longer liked the odds, and could no longer justify to himself all the physical travails that would continue to be required to maintain those odds.

This adds to the legacy of his 2026 title, that I for so long didn't believe in. It was such a tightrope act that it's made the greatest rider in MotoGP history go 'OK, that was crazy - crazy enough to call it a day'.

Absolutely the right decision but a huge 2027 loss

Given everything his body has been through, everything he has achieved, this is absolutely the right moment for Marc Marquez to retire. He has nothing more to prove and there is no point risking yet more injuries. Totally, totally the right call.

But I am so, so, so gutted that we will now never get to see how him versus Acosta in the same team would have panned out.

Stoner's shock retirement months before Marquez arrived in MotoGP deprived us of one epic head to head, but was totally the right call for Stoner.

Now Marquez has deprived us of something that would have been even more epic.

But good for him. He's picked his moment perfectly.

The greatest I have ever seen

I'll keep it short and sweet: he has earned this moment. The amount of pain, suffering and ability to keep coming back again and again has finally taken its toll on him.

He retired on his terms, something that he may have thought might not have been possible just a few months ago with the state of his right arm. To win his 1oth world title through sheer mental strength and earn the right to be called the greatest motorcycle rider of all time is the perfect ending.

The greatest I have ever seen, what a pleasure it has been.

Stops any doubt about GOAT status

Marc Marquez's bombshell retirement will cement him as MotoGP's Greatest of All Time.

He was already that in my view - he's beaten many of MotoGP's other GOAT contenders to his first titles, and then won more after completing one of sport's great injury comebacks post-Jerez 2020 (and all the setbacks that followed).

But retiring now on his own terms ensures that nothing that happens in 2027 will change that.

Acosta was the only rider who I felt would have half a chance against Marquez on the same bike, and now Marquez won't be going head-to-head with him.

Had Marquez tripped up there - something not out of the question, given he'd have to adapt to a whole new formula and Acosta's enormous potential - that may have put an asterisk over his status as the GOAT.

Instead, Marquez has left the building and leaves behind a scrap to be MotoGP's new benchmark rider, a fight I wouldn't be surprised if his Ducati successor wins.

From a selfish point of view as an observer and fan of MotoGP, I don't want Marc to stop. But I get why it's happening. The mission is complete.

He's been through hell since 2020, fought back to the top of the mountain, got hurt a few more times along the way, and after dominating 2025 pulled off an unthinkable comeback in 2026.

What else is there left to achieve? How many more times should he risk destroying his body just because his presence in MotoGP is box office?

Of course I'd have loved to see him up against Acosta on equal machinery. But we'll just have to add that to the long list of epic head-to-heads we've narrowly missed out on in many forms of motorsport dating back decades.

Marquez has carried MotoGP on his shoulders for long enough. Those shoulders deserve a break, and now it's time for new stars to lead the series into its Liberty-owned era. Who's going to step up?

I expected to be making a coffee at the start of FP1, not watching the greatest MotoGP rider of all time announcing his retirement on some slides.

Taking a step back, this shouldn’t really be as shocking as it is, and yet we’re all speechless. This is a man whose body has been battered by countless injuries and surgeries over his career, but especially the last six years. This was a championship which came from 102 points back after yet more injury.

He’s now stepping away at the very top of his game, coming back from years of turmoil to reclaim his crown - not just once, but twice.

It is, of course, a shame that we won’t see Marquez vs Acosta, that much awaited battle between the king and the heir.

But whatever happens, it is beyond doubt now that Marc Marquez did it better than anyone else.

Blah blah blah, yeah yeah yeah… but ten.

He's never seemed so physically spent

Friday’s FP1 is usually a lower key ambience to kick off the weekend. But the eerie silence as the camera cut to Marc Marquez let us know something was up.

Ever the maestro of conducting the media off track, it was simple but utterly shocking to read the words 'This will be my last race in MotoGP'.

I expected a playful '…for 2026' to follow on a final card, but no. This is the end - mercifully, on track, on his own terms.

We will not see Marc on the next generation of MotoGP bikes. There will be no Honda reunion and no head to head with Pedro Acosta as Ducati’s newest prince in waiting.

There will not be an 11th world championship title. But for all the tantalising future narratives we lose, what an extraordinary chapter of MotoGP history we have witnessed.

The talent hasn’t diminished, the mind is sharper than ever, but the injuries have now clearly taken a toll too far to continue.

Reflecting on his 2026 season, Marc has never seemed so physically spent after his sessions, so there is a logic to this timing.

The 1000cc chapter closes, he has given everything, leaving this extraordinary sport battled-scarred but having made an impact as one of the true legends of motorcycle racing.

Someone give Gigi Dall’igna a hug, he’s had an emotional 24 hours.

Robs us of tantalising Acosta battle in 2027

In many ways, Marquez’s retirement makes sense: he arguably has nothing more to achieve, his body is already broken enough, and a retirement on his own terms is nothing less than he deserves.

I feel quite sentimental about the end of this chapter though. Hearing Marquez’s story about his attempted comeback in Jerez after that 2020 crash is what got me into MotoGP. Following along with his journey back from all of those injuries and struggles at Honda to his successes with Ducati has been incredible to watch.

He’s also cemented his status as the greatest of all time in my book, especially over the last two season. Could he have won again in 2027? I think so, but that’s something only he knows for sure.

So happy to have witnessed the (tail-end) of a stellar career and happy that he can end it this way. That being said, I’m slightly annoyed that we’ve been robbed of what could have been blockbuster battles between Marquez and Acosta at Ducati in 2027, and also extremely curious about what comes next.

I pity the first 'after-Marc' world champion

I sort of pity the first A.M. (after Marc) MotoGP world champion...

My main disappointment is we won't see if anyone could have properly overthrown him.

He'd so emphatically reminded everybody he was the best in the business that maybe he wouldn't have been beaten, of course. 

It'll just feel slightly hollow for whoever succeeds him as world champion because justifiably or not there'll probably be that little asterisk of 'well, he only won because Marc stopped'. 

I'm trying to consider a hypothetical F1 alternative that fits better than the obvious comparison of Nico Rosberg in 2016. 

Rosberg was world champion but he wasn't the best driver in F1 at the time. So he couldn't be 'dethroned,' but I don't think there was an overarching 'ah, man, it would have been good to see who could have beat him' at play there. 

With Marquez you know that MotoGP's losing the absolute benchmark. 

Go beyond the headlines and sign up to The Lean Angle, The Race's MotoGP newsletter. You'll get bespoke content direct to your inbox every Tuesday, plus the occasional one-off edition like today, where we had a special on the Marquez retirement news.

items.author: Andrés Chávez
items.content:
NY Post | Mark W. Sánchez: The Yankees are open to bringing in a catcher, especially if he’s a good defender behind the plate and hits from the right side. They may need to hurry up, though, because the market might be drying up: Tyler Stephenson returned to the Reds, Gary Sánchez committed his future to the Marlins, and Ryan Jeffers accepted the Twins’ qualifying offer. Sánchez goes through some of the Yanks’ remaining options, including Carson Kelly, Austin Hedges, Kyle Higashioka, and more.

Heavy: Jonathan Loáisiga agreed to sign a two-year deal with the Yankees this week. As it turns out, according to New York Post’s Jon Heyman, the reliever actually turned down a more lucrative offer from the Mets to return to the Bronx.

NY Post | Greg Joyce: With Paul Goldschmidt signing a one-year deal with the Mets, he wraps up a productive two-year stint with the Yankees. The veteran first baseman revealed the reasons why he decided to move in a different direction. “My top concern was not, ‘Hey, how do I go to someplace where I get the most playing time?’ ” Goldschmidt said Wednesday morning. “My concern was going to a team where it felt right … and just have an opportunity to be on a team that has a chance to win and is going for it. items.title: Game Preview: Knicks vs. Heat, November 27, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
Back in the 1990s, one way to preserve basketball games for the future was to record them on a VHS cassette. For all the younger folks, this was a big, chunky, rectangular thing that had magnetic tape on the inside. Whenever a game was on TV, you popped your cassette into the video recorder, pressed “REC,” and from that point on, you could rewatch anything you recorded whenever you wanted. Or for as long as the tape held up, for that matter.

My favorite recorded event back then was Game Five of the first round of the playoffs in 1999 between your New York Knicks and the Miami Heat. It ended with Allan Houston’s historic leaning jumper with 0.8 seconds to go, sending the top-seeded team coached by the Godfather of Schenectady packing and the underdog Bockers on an improbable run all the way to the NBA Finals. The tape wasn’t just special to me because of the historic shot or the basketball played with bad intentions back then. It was also awesome because it showed the Knicks beating the Heat. Sorry, Grandma, I know you taught me not to hate anyone, but those were the Heat, my favorite team’s biggest rival for years.

Now, before A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend thinks he can hold a candle to the guy Patrick Ewing once offered one of his kidneys to, let me make it clear: That was a different time, a different rivalry. Whoever experienced it firsthand knows what I mean by that. When the Knicks meet the Heat on Friday night for their fourth NBA Cup game of the season, it will be different, much different. Different players, different coaches. Heck, it all seems like a different world. But make no mistake about it—it’s still Knicks versus Heat. Which means the stakes are just a bit higher than in a game versus the magicians from the nation’s capital or the royalty from “The Big Tomato.”

Knicks get first look at Giannis on the Heat

Friday’s game will be particularly interesting because it gives the Knicks a first glimpse at the newest version of the Heat, featuring Greece’s national hero Giannis Antetokounmpo, who also happens to be one of the greatest and probably most unique basketball players this generation has seen. The project started pretty badly, with Giannis continuously reminding everyone who cared and everyone who didn’t that he dearly missed Milwaukee, the city he had called home for every second of his storied NBA career until then. Then the schematic issues befell the not-so-hot Heat, who struggled with spacing, players playing in new roles, and the daunting task of implementing a headstrong player with immense gravity into a completely new system. Defense? Haha, good one!

But after a 3-6 start, the second-oldest team in the league decided this wasn’t the way to ride off into the sunset. Or rather, their famous coach made plenty of adjustments. Erik Spoelstra, as we all know, is one of the best in the business. Not only at taking average rosters into the Play-In Tournament but indeed at coaching that sport with the orange leather. He inserted young Pelle Larsson into the starting lineup, found a spacing solution for the Heat, doubled down on their identity as a full-court, offensive-minded team, and then watched his guys reel off seven mostly impressive victories in a row (among them wins over Houston and Detroit) before falling to Philly on Wednesday night.

What can we expect from the Heat specifically? They love to get up and down the court and play at the third-highest pace in the entire league. Currently, only the Memphis Grizzlies score more points than Spoelstra’s squad, and the Heat do it by shooting a high percentage from the field, drawing boatloads of fouls, and making use of two post players. Yes, you read that right—post players. Both Giannis and A’ja Wilson’s boyfriend can effectively score with their backs to the basket, and despite many worries, they can actually coexist next to one another. One of them fills the dunker spot almost all the time, they rotate decisively in screen actions, and overall, Miami runs its sets fast and ferociously to get them rolling downhill. They don’t just set screens to see where it leads them; they want to get into an action quickly before any lanes can close.

Heat, Spoelstra have adjusted after bad start

It works, partly because the players around Giannis and that guy who made a habit last year of disliking the team that won a championship before him are all doing a good job in their roles. Klay Thompson adds shooting (43.2 percent from downtown), Swedish Swiss Army knife Pelle Larsson provides a little bit of everything, and playmaker Davion Mitchell has all of a sudden turned into one of the better point guards in the league at age 28, averaging career highs of 17 points and 8.6 assists per contest while also shooting 51 percent from the floor and 43-plus percent from behind the arc. The bench has some older vets more or less collecting paychecks so far, but Bobby Portis and Andrew Wiggins clearly have some talent. Apparently, that also describes Ryan Conwell, a stocky second-round guard who has been a pleasant surprise for Miami.

That whole group will definitely look to waltz into Madison Square Garden on Friday with the idea of showing the champs that they are a team to be reckoned with. Whether they truly are remains to be seen; there are plenty of things that could uproot the positivity currently sprawling across South Beach. But the Knicks better be prepared for a tough test, and not because they might still be missing some of their injured guys or because they are coming off an emotionally draining victory against Cleveland on Wednesday. Not even because A’ja Wilson might have taught her boyfriend a few more tricks this offseason after winning her fifth WNBA MVP trophy.

No, it’s going to be tough because it’s Heat versus Knicks. And even if that doesn’t mean what it did in the days of the VHS cassette, it still means something.

Who: Miami Heat (10-7) at New York Knicks (12-6)Date: Friday, November 27, 2026Place: Madison Square Garden, New York, NYFollow: @ptknicksblog and bsky

items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Liam Delap can exploit Chelsea’s defensive woes while Senne Lammens is under pressure against Brentford

Nottingham Forest’s last couple of seasons have been a story of good runs and bad runs, but it may help to know that last season’s encounters with Chelsea both presaged changes of fortune. After they lost to Chelsea in October, a seventh defeat in 10 winless games, Forest’s form improved and they won seven of their next 12 in all competitions. But after beating Chelsea in May, their seventh victory in a 10-game unbeaten run, Forest’s form dipped dramatically and they have won only twice since. Oliver Glasner’s criticism of players whose “standards [are] not high enough” is clearly designed to raise them. Time will tell if it has worked but the key man this week is one who should have no issues with motivation and whose English is at least decent. Liam Delap, facing the side that signed and swiftly discarded him, could really trouble Wesley Fofana and Levi Colwill. The Chelsea centre-back pairing were described as playing like “two novices” by Jamie Carragher after they were outfought by Dominic Calvert-Lewin last week. “Until they sign that dominant centre-back and leader, they’ve got absolutely no chance of achieving anything,” Carragher concluded.

Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil. Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United, whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

items.lbText:
Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I ’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.

Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille , wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”

This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”

Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”

Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”

The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”

Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”

That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”

Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”

This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”

Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.

There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”

Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”

Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux , the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”…

items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
Our next reader Q&A is here! This time you can pose your questions not just to our team, but to an actual current pro, Australia's Michael Matthews.

We're going to catch up with Matthews next week at the Jayco AlUla team camp, and we're going to ask him exclusively YOUR questions for the next instalment of our series.

Now in his 18th year as a professional, Matthews has had a rollercoaster season to say the least, starting the year with a win before suffering a nasty crash that saw him break both his arms. Impressively, the 36-year-old came back for the Tour de France, where he was regularly in breakaways, and has packed in lots of racing in the latter part of the season, perhaps catching up for lost time.

Next year, he will race for Jayco AlUla once more, where he remains one of their top riders and someone who can excel on all types of terrain.

As a veteran of the peloton, Matthews knows the ins and outs of the sport and its politics, especially how it's changed over the last two decades, and how riders like him have to evolve with the rapidly changing nature of the sport.

items.title: Why Aprilia really wants the MotoGP constructors title, while Ducati could hardly care less
Is this cycling’s ‘Moneyball’ moment? Inside the arms race for UCI points
items.author: James Witts
items.content:
"After my presentation in Barcelona, teams wanted to chat and compare their models with mine. This is a growing field, whether it's in search of points or simply improving performance as a whole." That's Louis Van Gaelen. The Belgian's undertaking a PhD in health and artificial intelligence at the University of Antwerp. As a side project, the keen cyclist dug deep into professional cycling and, as his presentation at this year's Science & Cycling Conference revealed, 'roster optimisation for maximal UCI points'. It's not the sexiest of titles, but Van Gaelen's hobby, aligned with the work of an increasing number of data scientists around the sport, is proving critical for not only a team's success but their survival. It's time to talk about the merits of not aiming for victory…

How does the system work?

The current UCI promotion and relegation system, rolled out in 2020, works in three-year cycles with 18 licences available to the men's WorldTour. The Women's WorldTour has 15 licences; however, demand for these spots is less competitive due to the limited number of teams willing to make the step up.

The 2026 season was the first season in the latest cycle, meaning points earned up to the end of 2028 will determine the WorldTour line-up for 2029 to 2031.

"All points from UCI-sanctioned races count towards the team total, but only the points accrued from the top-20 scoring riders," Van Gaelen adds. "Remaining at WorldTour can make or break a team."

That's because WorldTour status guarantees teams entry into cycling's biggest races, including the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España. Relegation means losing automatic invitations, reducing television exposure, sponsor value and commercial income. It also makes attracting top riders harder, potentially creating a vicious circle of declining competitiveness.

The UCI also assesses a team's non-sporting side, including the financial stability of the team, which is why they granted Team Picnic PostNL a truncated 12-month licence for 2026. At the time of the ruling, the Dutch team hadn't finalised medium- to long-term backing with one of its sponsors, leaving the required fiscal guarantees for 2027 and 2028 incomplete. The Picnic turbulence continues to this day, heightened by serious allegations about team culture, with December 8, 2026 a key date in the calendar, as that's when the UCI is expected to confirm 2027 registrations.

But let's return to sporting criteria, as that's why the likes of Van Gaelen are in demand. His work looked to answer which riders a team should sign; which races each rider should participate in; and how a team can maximise its total UCI points across a season. The search involved combining two technologies: machine learning and mathematical optimisation.

Machine learning utilised 10 seasons' worth of data, covering thousands of riders and their previous performances, in addition to race profiles and course difficulty. "Inputting the course profiles was a laborious job," Van Gaelen says. "It involved uploading many, many course GPX files from an internet forum." Van Gaelen's machine-learning model then predicted the likely finishing order of riders in individual races, which were translated into expected UCI points using the relevant race's points scale.

The second part, mathematical optimisation, aimed to build the perfect roster by, for instance, matching climbers and sprinters to races where they're likeliest to score, by reducing clashes between teammates and setting a race-day ceiling at 85 days.

"With our optimised roster and focusing on one team in particular, we increased the points per rider from an average of 375.3 to 824.7," Van Gaelen explains. "Of course, there are limitations – our model didn't take into account fatigue, for example – but it's a promising proof of concept."

If Van Gaelen's work is good on paper, XDS Astana's is good in practice. The Kazakh team are the poster boys for optimising rosters in search of UCI points. At the end of the 2024 season, they were facing almost certain relegation, languishing 21st in the annual UCI rankings. But that's when they made one of their most important signings of recent times: data scientist Morgan Saussine.

One of the key implementations from Saussine's work was to prioritise top-10 finishes over individual victories. While historically teams would often organise their racing around one protected leader, with teammates sacrificing their own results to help that rider win, Saussine, who was unavailable for interview at the time of writing, identified there was much lower-hanging fruit to pick from in search of points.

Astana set about assembling a squad capable of scoring across different race categories, terrains and stages of the season. Into the squad came 14 new faces, including experienced riders such as Wout Poels, Diego Ulissi, Fausto Masnada and Mike Teunissen. The arrival of Chinese sponsor XDS provided additional financial resources to support the change. It worked, as they shot up the rankings to finish fourth in 2025 and so preserve their WorldTour status. Cofidis went down.

"Given the situation XDS Astana faced at the beginning of the 2025 season, when the team urgently needed UCI points, it's easy to see why a rider like Christian Scaroni was so invaluable," says researcher Simon Lucat. "Here's a rider who regularly finishes in the top-10 across a demanding race calendar."

Scaroni's importance to the cause was also highlighted this season with the 29-year-old Italian finishing inside the top-10 of one-day races or stages 33 times. He also won the overall at the Tour of Oman.

Lucat, a lifelong cycling fan and an economics student at Bocconi University in Milan, Italy, researched the inherent paradox that is professional cycling: results are attributed to individual riders, but they're collectively produced by a team.

"One of the main findings of my research is that the combined quality of the riders surrounding the leader can be just as important as the quality of the leader himself when it comes to accumulating UCI points," he says. "Strong teammates are valuable not only because they can help the leader achieve a better result, but also because they can score points themselves."

"The balance may also depend on the type of race," he adds. "Paris-Roubaix, for example, stood out in my analysis as a race where squad depth appeared to be particularly important. This makes sense if you think about the nature of the race, where a puncture or a crash can completely change a team's plans. Having several competitive riders gives you more options."

The original points detective

The likes of Van Gaelen and Lucat are building on the foundations laid by Raul Banqueri. In 2020, the diligent Spaniard waded through the UCI's 400-page road-racing regulations PDF in search of content for his Twitter account. It was needle-in-a-haystack stuff, but he pricked his fingers when he unearthed what many had missed. "I saw the UCI had started using sporting criteria to award licences and distribute wildcards to the WorldTour calendar," he says, "but almost nobody was reporting on it." He did, piquing the public's interest. And that of the professionals.

"When I started publishing my analyses of the points system, a multitude of WorldTour sports directors, performance directors and cyclists started following me on Twitter," he says. "Then in 2023 I started working with the Human Powered Health women's team. That season their licence was at risk, so I prepared a dashboard with advanced statistics on results and UCI points. We thoroughly analysed the calendar to identify which races they could score the most points in with the roster they had. The team focused more on flat races and minor races, tripled their UCI points compared to 2022 (from 914 to 3354) and managed to save their WorldTour licence.

"Nowadays, UCI points are no longer as important in women's cycling, as there aren't enough teams applying for the licence, but the dashboard remains valuable for the scouting process, signings and monitoring team performance."

That year, he also collaborated on projects with Visma-Lease a Bike, assisting the team's head of strategy, Patrick Broe, while in 2025 he saddled up with the Movistar Team women's squad, helping with data and video analysis. In short, Banqueri is hot property when it comes to delivering peak points and peak performance. So, what's his assessment of sniffing out peak points performers?

"Sprinters capable of getting over hills or specialists in hilly races with high top speed are increasingly sought after to claim points," he answers. "That includes Benoît Cosnefroy, Thomas Silva, Alex Aranburu, Natnael Tesfatsion and Lukáš Kubiš, who've all scored good points for their respective teams."

"In general, one-day races are significantly more profitable than stage races," he adds. "One-day races award the same points as the general classification of a race in the same category, and stages award very few points, except in the Grand Tours. Right now, I believe that ProSeries one-day races (250 points for the winner) are the most profitable in terms of UCI points."

Banqueri says an interesting development is the strategy and recruitment adopted by ProTeams, whose goal is the top 30 of the annual ranking in search of an invite to the Grand Tours. "These teams are the ones looking the most for races outside of Europe, especially in Asia, where the level is lower, since they can score a high percentage of their total seasonal UCI points. For WorldTeams, it's less profitable to travel to race in Asia, as it causes huge fatigue for their cyclists, and the UCI points they earn don't have as much impact on their total sum of UCI points.

"Also, some of the lower-level ProTeams, like Burgos BH, have signed cyclists from more immature cycling nations to take advantage of the UCI points they can win in National Championships and Continental Championships. All Continental Championships award the same points, as do National Championships, provided the nation participated in the previous World Championships. So, being the champion of Mauritius scores the same points as being the champion of France." To that end, five of Burgos BH's eight 2025 wins came at the national championships of Mauritius, plus Uruguay, Guatemala, Mongolia and Greece. In 2026, it was three from nine wins."

In both seasons, the Spanish outfit finished comfortably in the top-30, essentially guaranteeing them a wildcard spot at the Vuelta a España. These wildcard spots are keenly fought over for the same reasons that teams strain to cling onto WorldTour status, namely media exposure and sponsor value.

Downside of chasing points

For ProTeams, this short-term points grab could have long-term consequences for the sport. "This year, Bardiani had the lowest average age (only 22.4 years, according to Pro Cycling Stats) and ultimately fell out of the top 30 in the ranking, meaning they won't be invited to the Giro d'Italia in 2027," says Banqueri. "It's a bit unfair because a team like Bardiani is essential for developing young cyclists. It means in the future they'll probably have to sign more experienced cyclists to ensure results."

If there is a future. Come the end of the 2026 season, veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi couldn't contain his anger at the points system, calling the UCI "incompetent". Reverberi told the TriCiclo podcast that with no guarantees of invitation to the world's biggest races – they'd raced every Giro d'Italia since 1982 – they could soon be out of business. "How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We've already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year."

The Italian team, who have nurtured the likes of Sonny Colbrelli and Giulio Pellizzari, are known for their attacking style. The UCI points system, Reverberi laments, is anti-cycling, encouraging top-10s rather than chasing glory in the breakaway. "The UCI is incompetent. They've destroyed cycling," he concluded.

He's not the only critic of chasing lesser places rather than the podium. This is from Jayco Alula's Michael Matthews earlier in 2026: "For me it's destroying cycling." And this from Serge Parsani, team manager at ProTeam Solution Tech NIPPO Rail: "It's undoubtedly an anomalous ranking."

EF Education-EasyPost boss Jonathan Vaughters went so far as to say that collecting UCI points was forcing teams to participate in too many smaller races, some of which had inadequate safety arrangements. "They're [riders] being pressured by team managers like me saying 'we've got to get points – hurry up.'"

In short, a system designed to reward sporting performance ends up discouraging teams from racing to win. It's an imperfect system. This is the result of professional cycling's imperfect business model where teams are almost wholly reliant on sponsors for survival. It's one reason why 24 teams have recently formed the Collective Cycling Group (CCG), aimed at reforming the sport and streamlining the calendar. We'll no doubt hear more of the CCG in the near future, but it does highlight the fragility of cycling at the top level. Then again, which successful organisation doesn't look to optimise resources for maximum value? Back to Lucat…

"I was also interested in the relationship between budget and team performance," he says. "You'd naturally expect wealthier teams to perform better because they can recruit stronger riders, but my findings suggest that differences in measured rider quality alone do not fully explain their advantage. A team's budget buys much more than just riders. Part of that advantage could come from better coaching, nutrition, equipment, medical support or logistics."

"Smaller teams cannot match the spending of the biggest WorldTour teams, so they have to be very smart about how they use their resources, whether in recruitment, race selection or the composition of their line-ups," Lucat continues. "This is where data analysis could be especially valuable for teams that cannot simply rely on having the strongest riders in the peloton."

In English football's top division, the three B's – Brighton and Hove Albion, Bournemouth and Brentford – are examples of sporting teams who have maximised data to punch above their collective weight. As Lucat says, if your budget is nominal, you must maximise every pound, dollar or euro. That said, one measure of success for every business is efficiency.

Just look at UAE Team Emirates-XRG. Their budget is an estimated £50 million per year – the highest in professional road cycling – but for that they've not only nurtured arguably the greatest rider of all time and dominated the rankings, they also finished third in the 2026 WorldTour budget efficiency table, put together by the website 'How to turn pro', which tracks the fiscal side of professional cycling.

Though we can't take the website's findings as gospel truth – they state that rider and team budgets are based on factors like the limited publicly available information – they do document sources, as well as featuring a public changelog and correction process.

According to the site, the UAE squad accrued 656 points per £1 million spent in 2026. That was behind second-placed XDS Astana – 749 points per million from an estimated budget of £ 23 million – and the most efficient team, Uno-X Mobility, whose 784 points per million came from an overall estimated budget of £ 16.7 million.

Keep scrolling, and you’ll upset Sir Jim Ratcliffe and his accountants, who continue to return very little on their sporting investments. Netcompany Ineos ranked 17th out of 18 in the efficiency stakes; their mooted £43.5 million resulted in just 300 points per million. Picnic were low on budget and efficiency – £16.7 million and 178 points per million – leaving them rock bottom.

Looking ahead, if Picnic survive into 2027, they have some catching up to do, finishing this season with just 2,822 points. Groupama-FDJ are the next WorldTour team, over 6,500 points ahead on 9,329, followed by NSN Cycling (9,624 points). At the ProTeam level, Tom Pidcock's Pinarello-Q36.5 team (12th in rankings) and Tudor Pro Cycling (17th) are the leading contenders for promotion.

Where does that leave us? All in all, professional cycling's points race has made data, recruitment and calendar planning essential tools of survival, not merely marginal gains. Yet when teams optimise for rankings rather than victories, the system risks distorting the sport it's meant to reward.

As Banqueri signs off, this is sport where the ultimate victory is victory itself: "Of course, teams without a large budget must seek a balance between performing in the big races, which have a greater media impact, and scoring points in minor races that give them peace of mind in the rankings. But UCI points are not the only important metric of a team's success. Movistar finished the season in 13th position but won La Vuelta. Surely Astana would have traded their season for Movistar's?"

Ferrari facing 'very challenging times' - Hamilton
items.content: <article>Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are facing "very, very challenging times" as a result of the series of on-track incidents between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.</article>
items.lbText:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are facing "very, very challenging times" as a result of the series of on-track incidents between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.

The two drivers had talks on Thursday after arriving at the Qatar Grand Prix to discuss the fall-out from their collision in the race in Las Vegas last weekend, which team boss Frederic Vasseur said was "completely unacceptable" .

Both said the conclusion of those discussions would "stay internal" but admitted a solution needed to be found.

Hamilton said: "I like to think that we're stronger from these difficult...

"If everything was just great all the time, I don't think you learn anything when you're winning all the time. You learn really through the hardest times.

"These are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Charles and I."

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Leclerc admitted that "at the moment it's not working" and said there was "tension around that we need to dissipate".

The incident in Las Vegas was the second in three races between Hamilton and Leclerc .

In Mexico City last month, their battle on the first lap led to them handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen in a race that Ferrari should have finished one-two.

After that event. Hamilton said Ferrari "had to have some serious talks behind closed doors" and that the team had "big, big problems".

They had those talks in the next race in Brazil, brokered by Vasseur, only for there to be two flashpoints in Las Vegas.

Hamilton was first penalised 10 seconds for gaining an advantage by cutting the track while racing with McLaren's Lando Norris, in an incident to which Leclerc was also in close proximity.

And then Leclerc received a 10-second penalty for pitching Hamilton into a spin.

Leclerc said: "We have a very good relationship outside the car with Lewis.

"I wouldn't say the atmosphere was good because we are disappointed by the situation we are in.

"But we are all grown up and responsible and we have to find a solution and there is also a big willingness to find a solution."

Leclerc said the incidents kept happening because "we are two very strong drivers who want to finish one ahead of the other".

He added: "I do believe some level of tension is always there in top teams when you have two drivers.

"If you look this year there have been more than 10 times we have started side by side. We are always together. So a certain amount of tension is obviously always there, but it doesn't necessarily have to escalate and that is why we need to find a solution and fix that."

Hamilton added: "I have no doubts that next year we'll come back working hard together and in a better place. I think we'll quickly get better processes in place so that we can really get a right team."

Leclerc furious with integrity being questioned after Hamilton clashes
Russell finds Verstappen's criticism 'quite amusing'
items.content: <article>George Russell says Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and that he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".</article>
items.lbText:
George Russell has said Max Verstappen can "say what he wants" and explained he found the Red Bull driver's criticisms of him after the Las Vegas Grand Prix "quite amusing".

Verstappen said Russell was "so far below my level" after winning the race on Saturday.

His remarks were a response to Mercedes driver Russell saying "somebody has to stand up to this guy" after an on-track confrontation in practice.

Russell said before this weekend's penultimate grand prix of the season in Qatar: "I stand by what I said after practice, but he was the one who went out and won the race and I didn't, and I'm sure he had a bit of a laugh about that and it was reasonably amusing.

"He drove an incredible race and won it and he can afford to say what he wants."

Russell v Verstappen: F1’s New Rivalry Explodes in Vegas

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Asked whether he wanted to pursue reconciliation with Dutchman Verstappen, Russell said: "We're all competitors out there. There's no right or wrong way about the mentality everybody has.

"We are all different in many regards and you don't need to agree with one another. I'm not looking to be best mates with anybody on the grid. I am just working and looking and fighting to win. Simple as that."

British driver Russell said he had learned lessons from the incident in Vegas, which is the latest in a series of flashpoints between himself and four-time champion Verstappen dating back several years, and he might change how open he is with the media in future.

"It's all avoidable at the end of the day," Russell said. "It's all a bit unnecessary. It's not something I am looking to continue. I am not looking to have a poor relationship with people. That's not really the kind of person I am.

"There are lessons to be taken from these situations. Maybe I am just too open and honest with the media. I need to remember I'm talking to a camera that is broadcasting to millions of people. That's the biggest takeaway.

"It is not a war of words off track. I maybe have been guilty of being too open and honest when I speak with you guys.

"I feel like I have a good relationship with the media and I sometimes forget I am not talking to one person - I am talking to millions of people on the television.

"That good relationship has probably hindered me a bit and that is life lessons. I respect Max immensely for his driving talent and what he has achieved on track."

items.title: 'When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly' – Thibau Nys and Lucinda Brand's cyclo-cross team find new sponsorship from 2027 onwards
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team has swiftly found a new title sponsor following the withdrawal of Glowi, owner of named sponsor Het Poetsbureau.

The team, which is led by women's world champion Lucinda Brand and men's European champion Thibau Nys, welcomes electrical retailer Elektro Loeters as a new title sponsor alongside Baloise Verzekeringen.

The new sponsorship will begin on January 1, 2027, though the length of the deal hasn't been announced.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day," team manager Sven Nys said in an Instagram post announcing the news.

The deal came about quickly, the team confirmed, with Elektro Loeters only approaching them in recent weeks.

"When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly. We immediately felt a connection with the team’s vision and ambitions. Five days later, an agreement was already on the table. It shows just how similar entrepreneurship and top-level sport are."

The team, currently known as Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions, have been the most successful during the 2026-27 cyclo-cross season so far with 12 victories.

Nys has four wins, including three rounds of the X2O Trofee, while Brand has six, including two apiece in the X2O Trofee and Superprestige. Both triumphed at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam earlier this month.

Like the team, Elektro Loeters is also experiencing success, with the company planning to open five new stores in Flanders in addition to its 10 pre-existing stores.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day. Their growth story, entrepreneurial spirit and drive are a perfect match for our values. We are therefore looking forward to further developing this partnership over the coming months and putting it into action together," said Sven Nys.

Brand and Thibau Nys will lead the team in their new identity alongside other key riders Pim Ronhaar and Annemarie Worst. However, this will be Brand's penultimate cyclo-cross season, as the Dutchwoman will retire from racing in April 2028.

You Can Now Buy a 28-Gram, CNC-Machined Titanium Dynamo Taillight—If You’re One of 30 Buyers
items.author: Josh Ross
items.content: Berlin-based Allygn upgrades its EdelMü rear light from aluminum to high-polished titanium while keeping the same German-made Busch & Müller electronics inside.
items.lbText:
Berlin-based component brand Allygn has released a limited-edition titanium version of its EdelMü dynamo taillight, swapping the standard model’s aluminum housing for CNC-machined titanium for an extremely limited initial run.

The point of this kind of titanium extravagance is obviously to look great, but it does also solve a problem. For riders building custom randonneuring, bikepacking or commuter bikes, dynamo lighting has always been an aesthetic mismatch. While SON’s Edelux headlights are a staple on handmade builds, rear dynamo lights tend to look like an afterthought. Allygn founder and Fern Bicycles framebuilder Flo Haeussler originally designed the EdelMü to close that gap, taking the proven German-made internals from a Busch & Müller Mü taillight and housing them in a small, machined barrel that echoes the look of the Edelux.

It’s a natural problem for Haeussler to solve, as it’s the stated driving force behind the brand. Allygn Components specifically aims “for a fully integrated bicycle design, where every part blends seamlessly into each bike’s overall concept, both functionally and aesthetically.”

Which is why, as good as the EdelMü is, the new titanium version goes even further. The design keeps that exact formula but upgrades the outer shell from 6061 aluminum to high-polished, CNC-machined titanium.

Inside, nothing changes from a functional standpoint. The light ships with standard 6V AC dynamo internals from Busch & Müller, complete with capacitors to keep the stand light illuminated when stopped at intersections. Allygn says the housing can also accommodate 5-15V DC Mü internals for riders running e-bike or battery setups. Small cutouts machined into the titanium body provide side visibility.

The light measures 30.2 mm long with a 20.6 mm diameter at the plastic holder, and Allygn lists the weight at 28 grams including the uncut wiring and M3 bolt. Hardware consists of black zinc-nickel-plated stainless steel M4 and M5 bolts.

Two mounting configurations are available: an M6 direct braze-on option for custom frames and a POM ring mount. The ring-mount version is designed to pair with the rear light mount from fellow Berlin outfit Drust Cycles. Framebuilders can also source braze-ons directly from Allygn.

The titanium EdelMü taillight retails for €150, or roughly $142 for U.S. buyers through Fern Bicycles after German VAT is deducted at checkout (before any applicable import duties). A bundle pairing the ring-mount light with a matching titanium Drust Cycles mount is also available for €185.

Because only 30 lights are included in this first batch, availability is tight. Riders and builders can order through the Fern Bicycles website or contact Allygn directly for more information.

items.title: Huge Black Friday discounts on Shimano road groupsets at Sigma Sports, with 105 Di2, Ultegra and Dura-Ace all better than half price
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
Shimano is one of cycling's biggest component brands, best known for its extensive range of groupsets covering road, gravel and mountain biking.

The brand's range-topping Dura-Ace groupset delivers the highest level of road performance, with a race-proven design trusted at the biggest events in the world. Ultegra offers much of the same functionality at a lower price and with only a small weight penalty, making it a popular choice for performance-focused riders. Meanwhile, 105 brings electronic shifting to a more accessible price point, appealing to budget-conscious racers and endurance riders alike.

Fortunately for UK shoppers, there's currently more than 50% off Shimano 12-speed Di2 road groupsets at Sigma Sports, covering everything from 105 to Dura-Ace.

To suit a range of budgets and prices starting at just £699, there are some particularly good deals to be had here.

Shimano's Dura-Ace, Ultegra and 105 groupsets are all 12-speed and feature electronic Di2 shifting, with a semi-wireless set-up across the range. Each offers a slightly different balance of weight, performance and price, but all are currently considerably discounted at Sigma Sports with over 50% off.

Shimano's flagship groupset is designed for the demands of professional racing. It's lighter than Ultegra, but the two share much of the same technology and performance, meaning the decision to go for Dura-Ace often comes down to weight, aesthetics and having the very best. If you've got a frame that deserves a top-tier build, it's an easier justify - especially with 53% off bringing the price down to just £1,699.

For most riders, Ultegra is arguably the sweet spot. It delivers almost everything Dura-Ace does, with excellent performance and a well-considered design, but trades a little extra weight for a considerably lower price. At 278g heavier than Dura-Ace, it's a small compromise for the money saved.

As an upgrade or a more affordable entry point into electronic shifting, 105 Di2 is a great buy. It retains the 12-speed functionality and semi-wireless set-up of its more expensive siblings, bringing much of the same experience to a lower price point.

This is a great opportunity to upgrade to Shimano's 12-speed Di2 electronic shifting for considerably less than usual.

Our CN Lab testing also found the GP5000 to be faster than many competitors, including the pro-favourite Vittoria Corsa Pro. That makes them a great choice for performance-focused road bikes, while their impressive lifespan and built-in wear indicators add to their appeal, making it easy to see when it's time for a replacement.

Although many pros are adopting even faster TT-specific tyres for road racing, for all-round use (and when you are paying for your tyres), we still think this is the way to go.

For UK readers, Merlin Cycles has a very tempting deal on a bundle for just £99.95 down from £182, which includes a pair of the tubeless-ready tyres and 500ml of Stan’s Tubeless Sealant.

For US readers, there's no equivalent bundle deal available, but you can still pick up the tyres individually on Amazon, with discounts of up to 18%. The exact saving varies depending on which tyre width you choose.

If you haven't yet tried this Tour de France stage-winning rubber, there's never been a better time to pick up a pair, especially with 500ml of tubeless sealant thrown in for under £100.

For US readers, there's no bundle deal available, but you can still pick up the Continental GP5000 S TR individually on Amazon, with discounts of up to 18% depending on your chosen tyre width.

Continental says the Grand Prix 5000 S TR sets the standard in road tubeless-ready tyre technology.

The proof is in the riding, and our own reviewers have put countless miles into testing road tyres across a wide range of conditions. The GP5000 S TR tyres came out on top, earning their place as our benchmark for premium tubeless road performance and scoring a near-perfect 4.5 stars in our in depth review.
