items.lbText:
The French side earned their first group win over troubled German giants as Bellingham and Betis also caught the eye

Bayern Munich have hit a snagging point, with injuries wracking Vincent Kompany’s squad just as the head coach returns to work following his own health scare. For Lille’s winner, to exact Bayern’s first loss of the season, Aleksandar Pavlović had an own goal for the ages, desperately chasing back to then somehow direct the ball into his own net. Bayern are 15th in the Champions League table, and with Harry Kane out until well into 2027 and 18-year-old Lennart Karl asked to lead the line, resources are stretched. Jamal Musiala, subject of club grandees Uli Hoeness and Karl Heinz-Rummenigge’s gripes over his contract in the light of his neurological condition, could also play only 15 minutes.

Praise instead is due to Lille, coached by Davide Ancelotti to their first win of the group stage. They are captained by 36-year-old Benjamin André, who played one of the best matches of his long career. “Underrated” in the view of Ancelotti, who worked at Bayern under his father, Carlo. “Tonight was something special, we played like a monster.”

Soccer’s world-leading content delivery machine continues to supply a high grade of entertainment. While critics carp against the group stage’s baggy format, Manchester United have supplied the thrills, the spills, the pratfalls. Following the pathos of Atlético Madrid and Como, a comedy of errors at Sporting, with Senne Lammens saving a penalty from Luis Suárez, being unable to save Suárez’s next spot-kick and then dropping the ball for the same player to equalise for a 2-2 scoreline that undersold the chaos . United’s second goal, Bruno Fernandes’s second, also came via farcical means, beating Kaique Pereira, the Sporting keeper, after a bobble off a divot in the Estádio José Alvalade’s surface that Fernandes had himself created when trying to keep his footing. A word, too, for Szymon Marciniak, who gave a strange, overly-fussy referee’s performance, ruling out two seemingly legitimate United goals.

Were United improved? It was difficult to gauge. “With a performance like today it’s the best medicine to prepare the next game,” said Mauricio Pochettino, possibly still jet-lagged yet already deep in the United reeds. His team are 19th in both the Champions League and Premier League.

Kevin De Bruyne’s return to the Etihad brought yearning from both player and former club. Manchester City’s struggles continue and De Bruyne, now 35, is not performing as desired for Napoli, while those from within City continue to push the idea of business as usual amid the limbo of those guilty charges, two empty tiers of the renovated stadium cast telling shadows. Playing in an unfamiliar orange kit for reasons of partnership with a fashion firm best known for football casual “clobber” only added to the surrealism.

“When you don’t win, you question everything,” Erling Haaland said following a 2-2 draw rescued by some Rayan Cherki magic . Among those questions is how Enzo Maresca is dealing with the succession and legacy of Pep Guardiola. Recent signs are unpromising.

In late 2026, the year of Harry Kane, another Englishman is setting controls for the Ballon d’Or. Jude Bellingham has never played a Premier League match but who in the world’s richest league could afford him? At half-time against PSV Eindhoven, Real Madrid were 1-0 down, and then José Mourinho threw on Bellingham. He scored only one of the five his team ran in, though it was spectacular; a volley bearing a light comparison to Madrid legend Zinedine Zidane’s goal in 2002’s final in Glasgow. “I think Zidane is much better than me, he’s much more elegant and he’s my idol,” said a humble Bellingham , while also dismissing talk of inheriting Kane’s crown.

Only their second season in the competition, their previous campaign coming in 2005-06, when Marcos Assunção, Ricardo Oliveira and Joaquín were the star names, Betis are sixth in the table with four wins from five. The knockouts beckon.

The 2026 vintage is full of experience, with Manuel Pellegrini, 73, coaching a team captained by Isco, 34, and still as inventive as ever. The star man in defeating Slovan Bratislava was the Colombian striker Cucho Hernández, previously of Columbus Crew. Two towering headers made sure Slovan remained bottom on zero points.

“I was convinced it was going to be a magical night for me personally,” said Hernández, who was returning after over a month’s absence. Troy Parrott faces a fight to get back in, having been the match-winner in Betis’s opening defeat of Lille. Wednesday was another night where Antony, a Manchester United escapee flourishing elsewhere was a major threat.

“We don’t need to sign players in the transfer window, it’s not our style to sign a player for just six months. Above all, we’re not afraid of anything. We’re confident in our abilities and our resilience … Are we going to start crying and complaining? No, that’s not how a team operates.” – Paris Saint-Germain’s chances of a third title in succession were lowered when Désiré Doué joined Khvicha Kvaratskheliain the ruptured ACL club. Their coach, Luis Enrique, remains unbowed but Wednesday’s 2-2 draw with Roma suggested certain vulnerabilities. A new-look front three of Maghnes Akliouche, Ferran Torres and Senny Mayulu started against the Serie A club.

Liverpool, following a 3-0 win at Club Brugge that belied the scoreline, are the highest-ranked English team in the standings in fifth and host Porto next time out. Arsenal, in seventh after their shaky draw with Dortmund on Tuesday, host Real Madrid in two huge Premier League-La Liga summits; Manchester City travel to Barcelona. Two top-eight surprise packages, Betis and Como, also meet.

items.title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Lefty Gomez
items.author: Matt Ferenchick
items.content:
The history of the Yankees’ franchise is generally one defined by hitters. Starting with Babe Ruth and Lou Gehrig, the franchise’s most recognizable stars are almost always position players, carrying forward to the modern day with Aaron Judge.

However, you cannot win 27 World Series title by throwing out just anyone on the mound. There are still plenty of all-time Yankee greats that were pitchers. One of them was Lefty Gomez, a Hall of Famer in his own right.

Vernon Louis “Lefty” Gomez November 26, 1908 (Rodeo, CA) February 17, 1989 (Greenbrae, CA) 1930-42

Gomez was one of a number of Yankees of his era to come from California, as he was born there in 1908. His father was of Spanish-Portuguese descent and was a cowboy on a farm north of San Francisco. The kid later known as “Lefty” grew up riding horses and milking cows.

In baseball, Gomez grew up playing local sandlot games and was pretty quickly identified as a talent. By 14, he was already getting noticed by the Pacific Coast League’s San Francisco Seals, although they passed on the young, still scrawny Gomez at that time. After his high school career ended, the Seals finally agreed to ink Gomez, although the pitcher had to win over his father, who wished for Lefty to go to college to become an engineer.

The Seals farmed out Gomez in 1928, but brought him into the fold for the following season. San Francisco manager Nick Williams was still very skeptical of the still thin and scrawny pitcher, but Gomez eventually broke into the rotation through undeniable performances on the mound. By the end of the season, he was the Seals’ star, leading the league in ERA. The Yankees eventually took notice and signed him in August, but kept him in San Francisco for the rest of the PCL season.

Upon reporting to the Yankees for 1930, the team had similar concerns about his frame. They sent Gomez to a “health farm” during spring training. However, he impressed enough to start the year in the big leagues with the team. However, he struggled during his rookie campaign. Not only was he a rookie, but Gomez had suffered an injury after getting hit in the face with a liner back in spring training. Doctors suspected that botched dental work in the aftermath of that had caused an infection that was still bothering the pitcher. Gomez eventually got all his upper teeth pulled and replaced and eventually got sent down to the minor league St. Paul Saints.

After a year there, Gomez came back up to the Yankees in 1931, albeit put in the bullpen by new manager Joe McCarthy. However once again, Gomez battled his way into the rotation by simply being too good to deny. By the end of the season, Gomez had won 21 games while posting a 2.67 ERA.

Now a full-fledged star of the rotation, Gomez won another 24 games in 1932, although stats like ERA had him a bit below league average for the season. However, his knack for winning got Gomez the start in Game 2 of that year’s Fall Classic, and he delivered. Gomez threw a complete game allowing just two runs, only one of which was earned. The Yankees won the game and the series in a sweep over the Cubs.

Over the years, Gomez became a star for the Yankees as they became baseball’s preeminent dynasty. Gomez helped the Yankees to four more World Series titles over the course of his career, as they won a then-record four consecutive titles from 1936-39. Not only did Gomez win five championships in five trips to the Fall Classic, but he put up a perfect 6-0 record as a pitcher. That’s both a World Series and an MLB postseason record for the most wins by a pitcher without having ever taken a loss.

Individually, Gomez made seven consecutive All-Star teams from 1933-39. His best year came in 1934, when he won a league-leading 26 games, while also besting baseball in stats like ERA en route to the classic pitching Triple Crown (he won another in 1937), as well as modern ones, including 8.4 rWAR.

Gomez also became known as one of the most colorful characters in baseball, getting the nickname “Goofy.” While Yogi Berra has the most notable quotes of anyone in Yankees’ history, Gomez shouldn’t be far behind. Some of his best include replying to a question about whether he would brush back — another thing he was known for — his own mother with a pitch by saying, “You’re damn right I would. She’s a good hitter.”

Once while facing Bob Feller, Gomez — a horrifically bad hitter, even for a pitcher — lit a match. When asked by the umpire, “Do you think that match will help you see Feller’s fast one?” Gomez said, “No, I’m not concerned about that. I just want to make sure he can see me.” While filling out a job application following his retirement, Gomez listed the reason for leaving his prior employment as “Couldn’t get anybody out.”

In 1939, Gomez suffered an arm injury while covering first base, and that would be the beginning of the end for him. The injury began to affect his pitching motion and he was limited to just 263.2 total innings over the course of the 1940-42 seasons. He did pitch well in the middle of those seasons in 1941, but McCarthy somewhat controversially didn’t use him in the World Series victory over the Dodgers.

The injuries eventually caught up to Gomez, and the Yankees released him in January 1943. He signed with the Boston Braves but was released before ever appearing in a game for them. He was picked up by the Washington Senators, and appeared in one game for them, but was released by them too, marking the end of his baseball career.

Gomez eventually found his way into coaching and managed in the Yankees’ minor league system, including helming a team with a young Whitey Ford. He later left coaching and had a sales job with Wilson Sporting Goods. Thanks to his affable nature, he also became a popular dinner speaker and talk show guest. Gomez was voted into the Hall of Fame by the Veterans Committee in 1972. He eventually settled back in his native California, where he resided until passing away in 1989 at age 80.

Lefty Gomez was an undeniably great pitcher. However, it’s debatable whether he would’ve been as well remembered had he not been a member of those great Yankees teams and was putting up those stats for a middling one. However, he was a reason those Yankees’ teams were as good as they were. After all, you can’t win championships with outstanding talent on just one side of the ball.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here.

items.title: Lammens - the Man Utd goalkeeper under scrutiny like never before
items.content: <article>Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens made two major mistakes in the 2-2 draw with Sporting - could Mauricio Pochettino drop his goalkeeper?</article>
items.lbText:
After a first season at Manchester United that drew little but praise, goalkeeper Senne Lammens is under the microscope like never before.

A bad mistake that gifted Sporting their second goal on Wednesday, having earlier conceded a clumsy penalty, followed several other errors so far this season.

The 24-year-old Belgium international also made an error at the World Cup in the summer, spilling a shot that led to Spain's winning goal in the 88th minute of their quarter-final.

"I don't know [at what point Manchester United drop him]," legendary Manchester United goalkeeper Peter Schmeichel told CBS Sports on Wednesday.

"Mauricio Pochettino has come in and brought his own staff. That means he's got a new goalkeeping coach and maybe that is something that can change it for him.

"[At the World Cup] he came on against Spain and made a bit of a mistake. Mikel Merino scored and they got knocked out. I feel he's lost a little bit of confidence from that mistake and hasn't really recovered.

"As a goalkeeper, when you're not on your best form, you need your defenders in front of you to help you out. The sad truth is that they haven't been able to do that and that makes it so much worse. I like him a lot but today was not a great day for him."

Director of football Jason Wilcox and United's data team overruled Ruben Amorim when they opted to sign Lammens from Royal Antwerp for £18.1m in September 2025.

Amorim wanted Argentina World Cup winner Emiliano Martinez, who was left waiting for a deadline day call that never came to seal a move from Aston Villa.

United felt Lammens had the attributes to become one of the world's best goalkeepers. At 24, he is still young. Schmeichel was 27 when he joined United in 1991. Edwin van der Sar was 34 when he left Fulham in 2005. Both had hundreds of senior appearances behind them. Lammens has just over 100, more than half of them with Royal Antwerp.

Although he made the odd error last season, Lammens did nothing to suggest Wilcox and co had got it wrong.

After releasing Turkey international Altay Bayindir, who replaced Andre Onana as first choice at the start of last season and is back on loan in Turkey with Trabzonspor, they signed 36-year-old Wales international Karl Darlow as back-up this term.

Darlow finished last season as first choice at Leeds. But he only started 30 league games in three seasons with the Elland Road outfit. Also on the bench in Lisbon was Tom Heaton. The 40-year-old has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Mistakes earlier in the season – former United midfielder Paul Scholes claimed in September '"the jury is still out" on whether Lammens is truly top class – have brought increased analysis. His positioning for Dominik Szoboszlai's opening goal for Liverpool on Sunday was questioned externally, even if United focused their attentions on Bradley Barcola shoving into the wall.

Just 75 seconds after getting down to make an excellent save from Luis Suarez's first penalty, Lammens recklessly charged out and upended Maxi Araujo, even though Noussair Mazraoui seemed to be in a position to deal with it.

Then, after two Bruno Fernandes goals at the start of the second period had turned the Champions League tie in the visitors' favour, Lammens reached to collect a high ball and inexplicably dropped it in front of Suarez, who applied the overhead kick finish.

Understandably, there was sympathy in the dressing room.

"This team is a family," said striker Joshua Zirkzee. "There's no-one who will suffer by themselves.

"Senne is a great goalkeeper and mistakes happen. In this moment, we just give him space. I'm not sure if he wants to hear anything at all. But Senne's a great kid. He's got a good head on him. We didn't draw because of him, and we all know that next game he is going to be at the top of his game."

Toni Jimenez is Pochettino's long-time goalkeeping coach.

His arrival triggered the exit of Craig Mawson, who had been with Manchester United since 2019. Connor King is Jimenez's assistant but a relative newcomer himself, having joined from Burnley in 2026.

By its nature, goalkeeping at the highest level can be a mental challenge as well as a technical one. As Onana discovered, flaws can quickly become major issues and once the spotlight is shining, the attention is fierce.

Lammens has given the impression privately of being strong. He has seemed remarkably unaffected by his World Cup torment – his mistake against Spain came after he was introduced as a 71st-minute replacement for injured veteran Thibaut Courtois with the quarter-final delicately poised at 1-1. But only he knows the full picture.

Jimenez will be Pochettino's guide over what to do about the situation, although for now, Lammens' head coach is behind him.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

Following Wednesday's draw in Lisbon, Pochettino highlighted "two things" that need to improve if United are to start winning matches on a regular basis.

The first of those is the club's preferred goalkeeper. Of the 17 Premier League goalkeepers to have played a minimum of 10 matches in all competitions in this campaign, Lammens has the second-worst save success rate, keeping out just 60.2% of the shots he has faced. Only Coventry's Carl Rushworth (54.4%) has fared worse so far this season.

Lammens also ranks bottom of those 17 goalkeepers for clean sheet ratio (6.3%).…

items.title: Visma-Lease a Bike Just Lost a Title Sponsor – Here’s Why It Matters
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Visma-Lease a Bike confirms Visma is stepping down but will remain a partner as team hunts new finance to keep pace with Pogačar in the Tour de France arms race.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Anne-Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

Visma-Lease a Bike confirmed Thursday that the Visma IT company will step down as the team’s co-title sponsor in 2027.

But the brand isn’t leaving the team altogether.

Visma will instead be designated a “founding partner” next year. The team’s jerseys will feature logos of several Visma brands, and the business will continue to provide data and AI support.

The news marks a pivotal moment for the team of Jonas Vingegaard, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot, and Sepp Kuss.

There’s an escalating Tour de France arms race on both the men’s and women’s sides of the peloton, and the Dutch team needs to keep pace.

It’s been known since February that Visma was looking to reduce its contribution to the team. V-LAB management has been campaigning for a new co-title partner ever since.

The confirmation of Visma’s self-relegation Thursday – just one day after the “Killer Bees” expanded their collaboration with Nike – clears the way for a new backer to step in.

The team has not yet revealed who that might be. However, reports suggest further news might surface as soon as this week.

Visma joined the Dutch team as a secondary sponsor in 2019 and took naming rights in 2024.

The partnership aligned directly with Visma-Lease a Bike’s acceleration to the front echelon.

Primož Roglič went head-to-head with Tadej Pogačar and UAE Emirates at the 2020 Tour de France before Vingegaard won back-to-back yellow jerseys in ’22 and ’23.

Pauline Ferrand-Prévot was next to win the team a maillot jaune before Vingegaard completed his grand tour treble at the 2025 Vuelta a España and 2026 Giro d’Italia.

According to a team statement, Visma’s new designation as “founding partner” recognizes the role it played in the team’s development and its innovative, science-led approach.

“Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019. Since then, we’ve shared moments we could only dream of back then,” said team CEO Richard Plugge.

“I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years,” Plugge said. “Having Visma stay with the team as a founding partner reflects what we’ve built together.”

Visma’s backstep comes at a point when the team is struggling to keep pace with an escalating Tour de France arms race.

After Jumbo-Visma dominated at the turn of this decade, Pogačar and UAE Emirates-XRG blasted onto the scene with a blockbuster bank balance that helped buy wild success.

Pogačar has gone on to own the maillot jaune since 2024.

Meanwhile, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, Lidl-Trek, and Decathlon CMA CGM followed UAE’s lead with new backers, big budgets, and bigger signings.

On the women’s side, TotalEnergies-FDJ Suez went large with Demi Vollering.

It’s understood that Visma contributed around €20 million to Visma-Lease a Bike’s annual budget. The team was estimated to need a further €10 million on top of that to keep pace with its nouveau riche rivals.

Plugge told Feltet.dk this May during the Giro d’Italia he wasn’t in a sweat about filling a void worth €20 or even €30 million.

“The search is going well,” Plugge told Feltet about his quest for a new paymaster. “In my view, we are the biggest investment opportunity in cycling right now. A lot of brands and companies recognize that, which is positive for us.

“Together with our current partners, we have major plans for the years ahead,” Plugge said.

What the next step in Plugge’s plan looks like might become clear very soon.

items.title: 'The only way for the race to grow' – Women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs race becomes part of themen'sTour of Luxembourg organisation
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Organisers of the Tour de Luxembourg men’s race will take over organisation of the women’s Festival Elsy Jacobs from 2027, has learnt.

The race, named after the first-ever women’s World Champion, began in 2008 and has taken various formats over the years, even expanding to a three-day stage race. Under the new management, it will return as a two-stage race, moving from its traditional spot in the spring to take its place on the morning of the weekend stages of the men’s Tour de Luxembourg, scheduled for September 18 and 19, 2027.

The event will remain as a 2.1, third-tier event for the time being, though the new organisation has hopes of it moving up to the Women’s ProTour level at the earliest opportunity in 2029, joining the men’s event as a second-division race.

Since its inception in 2008, Festival Elsy Jacobs has been run by SAF Zeisseng, a local cycling club from the Luxembourg City suburb of Cessanges. However, since the 2020 race was cancelled due to the Covid-19 pandemic, the race has struggled, dropping the prologue in 2023 before becoming two standalone 1.1 races the following year.

"The change is the only way for the race to grow and not to disappear," organiser Michel Zangerlé told . "The association of the Tour de Luxembourg for men will take over, with us in support. That means we are not out, but the other organisation is the leader for every financial topic."

Despite the new structure, the race will retain its name, its heritage being important to the new organisation.

"It’s not Skoda Tour de Luxembourg Femmes or something like that; it will keep the identity of Elsy Jacobs," General Secretary of the Tour de Luxembourg, Benoît Theisen, told .

"We want to give the know-how we have in the men’s race and the setup of the men's race exactly the same as for the women. And for us, it was the only way to do it was to combine it in one date because if you have it on a second date, you need the full infrastructure again.

"It’s something new; we are really excited. It will be a new start, but we don't start from zero because there's this big heritage."

The original race would always have at least one day in Jacobs’ birthplace of Garnich, and while the 2027 race start and finish locations of the stages are not yet public, it’s highly unlikely this will continue, though clearly the race’s survival is far more important.

One of the issues the original organisation faced was the haphazard way in which the women’s calendar has expanded as the sport became more professional. Its regular place at the end of April meant that, since 2023, it clashed with the Vuelta España Femenina. That meant the race was no longer able to attract the biggest teams and riders, affecting sponsorship.

While it was never a big name on the calendar, the original organisation was always a trailblazer, introducing a live stream of the action as far back as 2017, when the majority of World Tour races were not shown live.

It has also been won by some of the biggest names in the sport, with Marianne Vos, Emma Pooley, Anna van der Breggen and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney all featuring on its palmarès.

Yes

Matte black, matte white

If you're riding an e-bike, going beyond the protection of a regular helmet is a good idea due to the additional forces at play from higher riding speeds and greater momentum.

items.title: Visma steps down as title sponsor of Visma-Lease a Bike team
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike have confirmed that Visma will no longer be part of the team name in 2027, with the Norwegian software company stepping down from its title sponsorship role but not leaving the team completely.

Such a move has been on the cards for months, and it was first reported back in February that Visma was looking to reduce the level of its investment, but the exact nature of the relationship from 2027 was made official on Thursday.

The team announced that Visma will become a 'Founding Partner' of both men's and women's teams, in a similar move to another former title sponsor, Jumbo.

"As part of this new partnership structure, Visma will no longer serve as the team’s name partner," read a statement from the team.

"The designation of Founding Partner recognises the role Visma has played in the team’s development since 2019, a period marked by continuous innovation and fantastic sporting success."

It is not yet clear who will step in as a co-title sponsor in 2027, with team management conducting an extensive sponsorship search for much of this year. As it stands, the team has simply been registered by the name of its holding company, Yellow B, in the initial application process for 2027 UCI WorldTour and Women's WorldTour licences.

Visma began its sponsorship of the team in 2019, and its title sponsorship coincided with a hugely successful period in which the team won 10 men's Grand Tours, including all three in the same season in 2023, and the 2025 Tour de France Femmes.

“It’s fantastic that Visma is extending its partnership with our team. Visma believed in our ambitions when we started working together in 2019," said team boss Richard Plugge.

"Since then, we’ve shared moments we could only dream of back then. I’m grateful to everyone at Visma for the trust they’ve placed in us over the years. Having Visma stay with the team as a Founding Partner reflects what we’ve built together."

Visma's CEO Merete Hverven was also quoted in the announcement, explaining that the company's "strategic priorities have evolved" as it has expanded from the Nordic region into Europe and Latin America.

Rather than the title nature of the sponsorship being brought to an end, this was framed within the context of several of Visma's subsidiary brands coming on board as minor sponsors from 2027.

"This strategic evolution is reflected in the updated partnership, where several of Visma’s leading national brands across Europe, offering accounting software for SMBs, will have their logos showcased on the team jersey next season.

Those sponsors will be revealed at a later date.

items.title: Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
It’s easy to get lost in today’s world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef.

As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him.

Jose Alvarado carries the Knicks to victory

There is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn’t on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can’t stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn’t rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan’s heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does.

It didn’t even take Alvarado’s tide-turning performance in the Knicks’ 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday’s NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the , “the most Mike Brown victory imaginable.” It didn’t take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year’s fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced.

Alvarado is not your type of guy? , says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn’t matter that he didn’t really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks’ bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don’t worry, bench guy, Mike Brown’s got a map, and he knows where to find you.

Mike Brown works his magic with the Knicks

With injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn’t have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn’t look out of place; he didn’t look like he didn’t know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions.

These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown’s doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn’t? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I’m sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get.

And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

Now this Chinese bike computer is on sale for Black Friday, and it offers performance that's on a par with far more expensive touch screen units. For me, it's an absolute bargain and our best budget bike computer right now.

Black Friday kicks off tomorrow, and the tech team is hunting for the best deals across all the sales.

If you are shopping for a bike computer, consider the BiNavi, created by iGPSPORT, sponsor of Groupama-FDJ United. This unit is easy to use, fast and powerful, with good mapping. I tested it for close to 1,000 miles this summer and was generally impressed with its performance.

The iGPSPORT app also works well and allows you to customise and update the computer unit.

This is a great price for a computer that performs as well as units that cost a lot more money.

Big colour screen, fast - what's not to like? Check out our review for a lot more information.

102g / 3.6oz 3.5” 32 GB Connectivity: ANT+ / Bluetooth / WIFI IPX7 35+ hours, depending on use.

It's fast, and the user interface is easy to use and navigate. It's compatibe with platforms like Strava and Trining Peaks which made it seamless when uploading my sessions.

If you wan't a computer for all your training and riding, and don't rely on mapping every ride. The BiNavi offers a solid platform and excellent value.

items.title: Lapierre on the brink of salvation with court studying multiple offers, as a former pro cyclist 'really wants to acquire' the French bike brand
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Lapierre is among the brands which Dublin-based Quanta Capital is hoping to save after the collapse of the Accell Group, can confirm.

Last week the Sunday Times reported that a deal to acquire the French bike manufacturer, along with historic British bike brand Raleigh, had been done, but the transaction is not yet complete, according to Lapierre's Directeur Général William Perrier.

Lapierre, which supplies bikes to the Picnic-PostNL team, was founded in 1946 and has been making bikes in the French city of Dijon ever since. It was bought by Accell Group in 1996, but since the parent company’s collapse in August of this year, it has been in court supervised administration, allowing a six-month observation period from September 21 to find new investment.

"We had some offers on the table, and more recently, beginning of this week, we were in front of the court to do a check after the offers and to have a clear status [on] where we are and what we still have to work on to make it happen," Perrier told .

"I will only comment the Lapierre part, but of course Quanta is one of the candidates, but from now on the court did not take any decision.

"We are looking at it, but I don't want to promise too much, right? We are still working on having a new owner, nothing is 100% signed."

Accell, which owned a number of other cycling brands, struggled after the Covid-19 pandemic. In late July it was due to be bought by the Singapore-based DuTech Holdings, but Accell was declared bankrupt five days later, and the deal fell through, leaving its brands high and dry, though DuTech has since acquired some of Accell’s other brands.

Led by former pro cyclist Mel Sutcliffe, Quanta Capital’s interest in some of Accell’s brands was rumoured and confirmed soon after the collapse, and now it seems close to fruition.

"So there is still some discussion between all the parties to check the financing part, the social part, the overall project in order to sign the deal. But as of today, of course, Quanta is one of the potential bidders who really wants to acquire Lapierre," Perrier continued.

"But this morning [Thursday, November 26] I can tell you that it is not yet the case. There is like a lot of discussion ongoing. We are still working normally, we are still producing bikes in Dijon. We are still delivering as much as possible [to] our dealers and our final customers."

Sutcliffe declined to comment when approached by and a request for comment has since gone unanswered.

British bike brand Raleigh was acquired by Accell in 2012, but although Quanta is confirmed as being interested in the brand, with the Sunday Times reporting the deal is done, there seems little left to save.

In late September the Nottingham Post reported that a total of 43 employees had been made redundant, with only two retained, and that the company’s remaining stock had been sold to UK Bike retail chain Halfords for more than £7m.

The administrators’ report stated: "No part of the trading business was transferred as a going concern as this was ceased immediately upon our appointment." That leaves the Raleigh trademark, which is still owned by Accell and its creditors.

items.title: Castelli's warmest winter cycling jacket is on sale, with one variant offering a mind blowing £272 saving in early Black Friday sale
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
The Alpha 150 is the Italian brand’s most wintery and most expensive outer layer best suited to long, steady rides at temperatures of around 7 and 12ºC (44-54 ºF).

At full price, it's a lot of money to spend on a jacket, but the Castelli Alpha 150 jacket is now available for less in both the UK and US with these Black Friday deals.

For UK readers, the men's Alpha 150 is 25% off in black, with most sizes currently available. The women's version has an even bigger discount, with 76% off the Hibiscus colourway in size XS, while the black version is 30% off across all sizes. In the US, the men's jacket is 40% off in black, dropping from $420 to $252, with other colourways discounted by 25%.

Our Senior Tech Writer, Will Jones, describes it as a warm, comfortable and highly breathable jacket, making it a great choice for cold-weather riding, although those regularly riding in freezing temperatures may want something more heavily insulated.

Castelli’s jacket range has gone on a fair old journey in recent years. The Gabba and Perfetto have been overhauled, and everything is now PFAS-free.

The main fabric of the Alpha 150 is Castelli’s exclusive ‘150g Polartec® AirCore™ electrospun air-permeable membrane’, which is alleged to be windproof while also remaining highly breathable. If it's going to rain, you'll want to wear something else though.

Open up the main double zip and you’ll reveal a Polartec Alpha inbuilt gilet which is very well executed. The rear panel is free-floating, attached only at the sides and top so it articulates more easily.

The form is tailored but not skin-tight, with enough room to layer up a little bit underneath, at least with a thicker long-sleeve jersey and a winter base layer.

Overall, this is a very good jacket that Will enjoyed wearing, offering a comfortable fit and excellent breathability. However, while it's a great option for cold-weather riding, its suggested temperature range may be a little optimistic. Will found that it wasn't particularly suited to temperatures below around 5°C, especially if you plan on stopping for any length of time.

items.lbText:
Rivals engage law firm Wiggin as they seek damages

Claim could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds

Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham are using the same law firm to prepare a legal claim against Manchester City for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds.

The clubs have engaged the services of the London-based media, entertainment and technology specialists Wiggin. Arsenal are using their retained lawyers, HFS Kramer, to prepare their own claim.

A source with knowledge of the case disclosed there had been a degree of cooperation between the clubs using Wiggin, because they have also engaged the same analysts to assess the size of the potential losses allegedly caused by City’s financial cheating , but that they would bring separate claims for damages.

“The cases are similar but different,” the source said. “The ultimate causation may be the same, but the damages will be different so they will be separate claims.”

Another source disclosed that Tottenham initially engaged Wiggin while Daniel Levy was the chair and were the first club to make legal moves against City after they were charged with financial fair play breaches in February 2023, with United and Liverpool following their lead.

Those three clubs and Arsenal lodged legal notices in November 2024 reserving their right to seek compensation against City to avoid their potential claims being ruled time-barred, one of the mechanisms through which City succeeded in 2020 in having a two-year ban from the Champions League imposed by Uefa for similar alleged offences lifted by the court of arbitration for sport.

Standard breach of contract claims have a six-year statute limitation from the moment they are made public, and with the allegations of City’s rule-breaking first published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in November 2018, four of the other members of the big six acted to reserve their rights.

Chelsea did not instruct lawyers to begin a claim against City at that point, and are not believed to have done so since, despite the fact that extensions to the time limit can be granted in cases of fraud and concealment.

The four clubs who are preparing legal action have stepped up their activities since the Premier League announced in September that City had been found guilty of the vast majority of more than 100 charges against them, with an independent commission ruling that the club had artificially inflated its income by more than £900m through the use of “sham contracts” between 2009 and 2018.

Tottenham are likely to make the biggest claim against City because they missed out on Champions League qualification to them on four occasions during that period, with dropping into the Europa League costing them more than £120m.

United and Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to City during years when City have been found to have inflated their income, in 2012 and 2014 respectively, costing them prize money and commercial revenue and bonuses.

Arsenal missed out on Champions League qualification by finishing fifth in the Premier League in 2017, the start of a six-season run outside Europe’s elite competition that combined will have cost them hundreds of millions of pounds, as City ended up third.

Arsenal also sold five key players to City during the period of their breaches – Kolo Touré, Gaël Clichy, Emmanuel Adebayor, Bacary Sagna and Samir Nasri – and may claim additional losses on the grounds that their purchases were artificially funded.

Everton, Newcastle and Chelsea also missed out on Champions League places during the relevant period, and numerous clubs including Hull were relegated in part owing to their results against City.

Stoke lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, costing them a Europa League place, and their then manager, Tony Pulis, said in October that the club should be awarded the trophy.

City have denied wrongdoing since being charged almost four years ago and have launched an appeal against the independent commission’s verdict , which will be heard by a new three-person panel next month. After launching their appeal in October, City issued a statement saying the commission’s judgment contained “multiple clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe” and that “the club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all its positions, relating to this case”.

items.title: The Magicshine SEEMEE 300 rear light boasts a huge 300 lumens and 200-hour battery life, and it's now 40% off for Black Friday
items.author: Emily Tillett
items.content:
The Magicshine SEEMEE 300 is one of the best rear bike lights we've tested, combining a wealth of features with market-leading battery life and a very reasonable price tag.

However, the SEEMEE 300 still has plenty going for it, with three key advantages over its newer sibling - longer battery life, additional side visibility thanks to its downward-facing LED, and, of course, a lower price.

Our Senior Tech Writer, Will Jones, found very little to fault with the SEEMEE 300, awarding it a near-perfect 96% score following his testing. Will only marked it down for the slightly confusing mode selections.

With 40% off for Black Friday dropping it to just £35.99 ($41.79 in the USA), it's an even more tempting buy.

It may have been superseded by its 400 sibling as our best rear bike light but this older model still does some things other lights on the market don’t in terms of battery life and additional visibility.

The SEEMEE 300 boasts one of the longest battery lives of any rear light on the market, offering up to 200 hours in Eco mode and comfortably outlasting its newer sibling, the SEEMEE 400, which tops out at 107 hours because of the higher overall power output of the 400 lumens.

It also offers great side visibility with the downward-facing LED on the underside that projects a red cone around you to make sure you're seen from all angles.

Smart features are now pretty frequently seen on the best rear bike lights and the SEEMEE 300 is no exception. These include an auto-dim function, which adjusts the light's output to suit ambient lighting conditions, helping to preserve its already impressive battery life. There's also a motion sensor that acts as a brake light, increasing the light's output when you slow down which is a particularly useful addition if you're riding in traffic.

items.title: The most dramatic moments of the 2026 cycling season – Shock retirements, nail-biting sprints and tense transfers
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
2026 is coming to an end, with training camps about to begin and attention already shifting to the 2027 racing season. Here at , we've already been reviewing many aspects of the season just gone, such as the best neo pros and best domestiques, but what about the moments that defined the year?

Rather than best moments – because who could ever choose just 10? – we've gone back through the headlines to identify the 10 most dramatic moments of the 2026 season, the stories that shocked all of us and the racing that got the excitement brewing.

From sudden retirements and high-profile crashes to tensions bubbling over at the biggest races on the calendar, as well as thrilling sprints and a debate about anti-doping, here are the 10 moments that we think delivered the drama in 2026.

Simon Yates' shock retirement

Rewind all the way to the start of the year, and things kicked off with a bang before the racing had even really started, with Simon Yates shocking the world with the news of his retirement. Rumours of Yates thinking about an early exit from the sport had been swirling, but after he'd won the Giro d'Italia, completed the 2025 season and started winter training and 2026 camps with Visma-Lease a Bike, it seemed like that must be off the table. Apparently not.

One day he was out training in Visma kit, and the next he announced his retirement just a few days into January. It was a surprise to not just the cycling world, but to his team too, who were then left scrambling and a rider short for the rest of the season. To bow out on such a high, as the Giro champion with a full and busy schedule, is practically unheard of and dominated the headlines for weeks as we collected reactions from around the peloton – mainly equally as surprised as we were.

Even to this day, Yates has not opened up all that much about why he made his decision when he did, instead just slipping back into normal life. Whilst it might not have felt that dramatic to him, it was certainly one of the defining moments of the first part of the 2026 season.

A frightening crash at Milan-San Remo Women

I wouldn't usually include a crash in a list like this, but if I am thinking of moments that were shocking and dramatic to their core, the scary crash involving Debora Silvestri, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Kim Le Court-Pienaar at Milan-San Remo Women was one of them. Coming off the Cipressa at high speed, several riders came down hard, with Silvestri the worst off as she crashed over the guardrails and fell several feet onto concrete.

This isn't the kind of drama we want to celebrate or remember, but it was a frightening moment that raised questions about safety, speed and risk – questions that would continue through the season. Silvestri's myriad of injuries and long stay in hospital, including needing breathing support, was a stark reminder of just how much danger cyclists face with very, very little protection between them and hitting the tarmac and over 60kph.

The intense debate about safety hadn't quite kicked off back in March, but it became a defining conversation of the 2026 season, and this crash will go down as one of the types of incidents we must work harder to avoid, or at least offer riders more protection from.

The final sprint of men's Paris-Roubaix

The final sprint of Paris-Roubaix is always one of cycling's most electrifying moments, and this year was no different, with the velodrome finales of both the men's and women's races offering spectacular, hold-your-breath racing. Franziska Koch bettering both Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot was an enormous underdog win moment in the women's race, but the one that will really, really stick with me is the climax of the men's race.

The whole race was packed to the brim with drama, to be truthful, but that was distilled into a few minutes of pure adrenaline as the leaders entered the Roubaix velodrome. Wout van Aert vs Tadej Pogačar. Knowing what we do about both riders it felt in a way like the story might already be written. Van Aert is the rider more likely to win Roubaix, given the reigning Tour de France champion is usually nowhere near the top of the list of favourites. But the mythology of these two riders made it different; Pogačar is the rider who wins at will, and Van Aert is the one who has been runner-up more times than you can count. I had a sinking feeling that the Belgian star was going to be denied yet again by the specialism-defying Slovenian.

That's why, when Van Aert drew slightly ahead of Pogačar in the sprint and soared to a fantastic win, it felt like a shock and a huge moment. It was somehow the obvious result and one that felt like it could easily slip through Van Aert's fingers, but it didn't.

Pogačar had been beaten – a very rare occurrence indeed – and Van Aert had scored his first cobbled Monument win in a wildly emotional moment. It was a gripping sprint to round out a hugely dramatic race, and is surely one of the most memorable moments of 2026.

Falling ice on the Colle delle Finestre

The penultimate stage of the women's Giro d'Italia should have been one of the most dramatic days of the women's calendar as they went up and over the Colle delle Finestre, but it ended up delivering the drama in different ways than we expected.

Instead of going up and over the mythical gravel climb and climbing back up to Sestriere for the finish, the stage was shortened mid-race due to the risk of falling ice of the top of the Finestre. This meant that the Giro's most epic stage was suddenly turned on its head, with riders having to adapt their tactics and plans on the road, leading to an all-out battle on the climb – which, ironically, might not have happened had the stage maintained its full length.

Four riders came towards the revised finish line together, with Demi Vollering powering away from Bella Holmgren, Antonia Niedermaier and Anna van der Breggen to pull closer to the overall lead, which she would go on to grab away from Van der Breggen on the final stage. All this unfolded in the ominous mist atop the Finestre, making for truly dramatic scenes.

Overnight testing debate at the Tour de France

The Tour de France hasn't faced actual doping drama for several years now, with a few unfruitful raids the most we've seen and a long way away from the mid-race positives and expulsions we were used to seeing a few years ago. But the 2026 edition still found a way to weave a controversial doping storyline into its plot.

The drama ended up not being about doping itself, but testing, when several top names including Pogačar and Vingegaard revealed that they had been woken in the middle of the night by testers. Gloss over the fact that riders aren't actually meant to reveal stuff like that – the anti-doping authority's element of surprise is a bit undermined if riders understand their tactics – and it was soon pretty much the biggest story of the middle of the race. Debate raged on over whether it was ethical to wake tired riders in the early hours as they tried to recover before another stage, and about whether this meant there was suspicion over the riders involved (to be clear, such tests do not imply any suspicion).

As far as we're aware, nothing came of those midnight tests, with the date for results to be returned long gone by now, but it certainly brought the topic of testing and doping back into the spotlight at the Tour, and stirred up the drama in a race that wasn't exactly full of that racing-wise.

Jonas Vingegaard crashes out of the Tour

The first of two really dramatic GC crashes over the summer, Jonas Vingegaard's Tour de France was over in the blink of an eye when he crashed heavily on a nondescript corner on stage 15. It was clear pretty quickly that he was not going to continue, as he clutched his arm in a way we all recognise as a surefire sign of a broken collarbone – an injury no one can race through. It was a shocking and sad sight, and heavily shaped the rest of the race.

Suddenly, the only rider who has ever challenged Tadej Pogačar at the Tour was out of the running, and even if he was already 4:30 down at that stage, any tiny hope of a miraculous turnaround was definitively gone. It felt like Pogačar's fifth win was confirmed in that moment.

As it turned out, that one crash would go on to have further reaching effects than we could have imagined at the time, with Vingegaard ultimately opting not to return to racing at all in 2026, and rumours even brewing that retirement was on his mind after another big crash in the sport he has already criticised for being too dangerous. Thankfully, he's since confirmed that he's not bowing out just yet, but that crash may still go down as a defining moment in his career.

A wild weekend in Nice to close out the Tour de France Femmes

If fans had felt that the Tour de France hadn't been dramatic enough in terms of the racing and results, the Tour de France Femmes came along and said 'hold my beer'. The start of the race was a bit of a slowburn, admittedly, but as we arrived in Nice for the final weekend, the temperature – both literal and metaphorical – was turned up to the max.

First was the bitter clash between Célia Gery and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney, with the Polish rider angrily confronting Gery and accusing her of deliberately blocking her in order to benefit Demi Vollering, with something of a war of words ensuing over the next 24 hours. On top of that, Marlen Reusser suffered a nasty crash on the final stage that saw her tumble off the podium – after previously being in the lead and fighting for the win – and roll into Nice heartbroken and in tears.

And that's all without mentioning the race itself, which saw three different riders wear yellow over the final four days, with a battle for seconds right up until the final finish line in one of the most thrilling editions of the women's Tour we've seen yet. It was tense and sweltering under the Nice sun, and feelings definitely boiled over at times, which is why this goes down as one of the most dramatic weekends of the season.

Tadej Pogačar crashes out of the Vuelta

The second major GC crash-out of the season was even more dramatic that Vingegaard's. Pogačar is a rider who crashes relatively rarely, so to see him go head-over-handlebars, whilst in the red jersey and the overwhelming favourite to win the Vuelta a España, was shocking and almost unbelievable, so rare is such an incident. We think a small rock in the road was to blame for one of the worst crashes of Pogačar's career, and not just because it dramatically took away his chance of completing his Grand Tour set, but because he suffered some truly nasty injuries. He suffered a concussion, a fractured collarbone, and three fractured vertebrae, having to undergo surgery and a significant stay in hospital.

The crash changed the course of the Vuelta – Enric Mas soared to victory in the race that looked nailed-on for Pogačar – but also the whole rest of the season, with new faces coming to the fore at the World Championships, Euros and Il Lombardia, races which the Slovenian has previously dominated. In many ways, Pogačar's crash was the defining moment of the latter part of 2026, and a healthy dose of drama for the rider who often seems to glide right past any misfortune.

Riders protest the start of Il Lombardia

I'll admit, I don't usually tune in for the flag to flag coverage of Il Lombardia, because what's actually going to happen in the first hour of such a long race? But it became clear pretty quickly that anyone not watching the start of this year's race had missed a surreal moment, as the riders staged a protest about rider safety. In many ways, what stands out about this moment is that, whilst impactful, it in itself actually that dramatic. There was no song and dance or outburst of frustration, just a quiet standstill in solidarity with the increasing dangers the peloton seems to be facing, and an emotive but firm speech from Remco Evenepoel.

But it was dramatic in the sense of being surprising and headline-making, and it was all anyone talked about for most of the day, until Paul Seixas took over the narrative with his emphatic win. It felt like – probably belatedly – something of a watershed moment, riders making it clear as a whole that the incidents that have affected the peloton this year are simply not acceptable, and setting out the possibility that riders may just refuse to race if changes are not made. It's been an issue that was brewing all season, and really came to a head in the final weeks of the year. Hopefully, that can manifest in real improvements in 2027 and beyond.

Paula Blasi exits UAE Team L'Imad

Our final dramatic moment was less of a single moment, but a dramatic saga that dragged out over the whole season, with various moments of tension before the situation was finally resolved in October. Paula Blasi should have had the best year of her career so far, winning La Vuelta Femenina and Amstel Gold Race in only her first full year as a WorldTour rider, but instead she became embroiled in a difficult and often very public transfer drama.

The Spaniard decided early in the year that UAE Team L'Imad was no longer the right environment for her, and though a relatively straightforward three-party agreement and pay-out would allow her to move to a new team – as multiple riders have done in the last few years – but what ensued instead was a fairly unpleasant struggle, with UAE attempting to block the move, talking Blasi down in the press, and supposed rider tensions becoming a particular sore spot at the Tour de France Femmes. This was all paired with trouble behind the scenes at UAE, who let go of their team principal prematurely and have struggled to find a full time replacement.

In the end, Blasi's move to Movistar did finally go through after a great deal of negotiating, and the 23-year-old seems to be much happier after reporting some really difficult times that even made her question whether she belonged in cycling. A year that should have been remembered for her breakthrough successes may well be remembered for this conflict instead, so she and her new team will be hoping it's only her results that make the headlines in 2027.

items.title: 'Ridiculous and stupid' – Mads Pedersen hits out at UCI contract rules which sees riders wearing old teams' kit to new team training camps
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Mads Pedersen has hit out at the UCI contract rule requiring riders to wear their old kit at their new team's training camps.

This week, Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz have been seen wearing Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and EF Education-EasyPost kits as they met up with NSN for the first time, and in the coming weeks we'll see more and more of these out-of-place kits during teams' December camps.

It's all down to UCI regulations, which mean contracts run to December 31, meaning riders are still representing their 'old' teams until the New Year. Regulation 2.15.139 reads, 'The riders may not, for the duration of the present contract, work for any other team or advertise for any other sponsors…'

Speaking on his podcast, Pedersen called the regulation "ridiculous and stupid."

"You could simply include a clause stating that in the event of a team switch from December 1 – or from the first training camp – you are allowed to use your new team’s equipment," he said.

"That would make it so easy. Then you wouldn’t have all that nonsense anymore, and you would prevent riders from missing out on their pay in December because they were riding a Ridley while contractually they were required to ride a Trek."

Pedersen will witness a host of riders in their old team's kit when his Lidl-Trek team meet up in Spain next month. Key new signings Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Jordan Jegat will be wearing Netcompany Ineos, Decathlon CMA CGM, and TotalEnergies kits.

"We are working on it with the AIGCP [the association of professional cycling teams] and the CPA riders' union," he said.

"The regulation change will definitely happen, with contracts starting on November 1. The starting year is yet to be determined in consultation with all stakeholders."

Riders and teams favour changing the rules, and the UCI was reportedly seeking to do so, yet the rules remain in place, drawing complaints from fans and the peloton.

items.title: Primož Roglič tempted by each Grand Tour in 2027, but a decision is several weeks away
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Primož Roglič has not yet made a decision on his race calendar for 2027, saying it was “way too early” given he only signed for his new team, NSN Cycling, little over a week ago. But he did say that all three of the Grand Tours are tempting him in their own way.

Roglič has won the Vuelta a España a joint-record four times, and he also has a Giro d’Italia title to his name from 2023, with the Tour de France the one missing from his palmarès.

Next year, the Giro d’Italia represents something of a draw, given the race heads into his native Slovenia, first on stage 1, then an entirely Slovenian stage the next day. The Tour de France, meanwhile, might represent some of that “unfinished business” he spoke about this week, especially after not racing it this year.

And the Vuelta of course is the Grand Tour where he has made his name and stands a chance of becoming the outright record holder with five titles, after showcasing his persisting Grand Tour credentials with the runner-up spot this year.

"Actually, we sat down together with the directors and a couple of guys, and then we started talking, you know," Roglič said during a first round of interviews from the NSN Cycling training camp in Spain this week.

"The Giro starts almost in Slovenia, the second stage is in Slovenia, the Zoncolan [on stage 20] is not far from Slovenia… nice.

"The Tour de France, I was not there last year. It’s missing me… nice.

"The Vuelta, you know… also nice."

Roglič has clearly started mulling things over but insisted no decision has been taken yet, saying he has other business to attend to first, namely meeting all his new teammates and staff, as well as familiarising himself with his new equipment.

"Later on, hopefully, yes, we start to make more seriously a deeper program, and from that, we can also define which Grand Tours I would like to do.

"We can also then make a [plan for the] start of the season, but for sure I will not start early in Australia or something like that."

NSN Cycling’s general manager Kjell Carlstrom also insisted it was too early to decide where Roglič will race in 2027, indicating that they will wait for the route for the Vuelta a España to be revealed on January 14.

"The other thing that we definitely want to see is the the Vuelta route and how that is designed because we believe that without knowing what the Grand Tours look like, it's impossible to build a complete calendar," Carlstrom told .

"Then you have to start from the Grand Tours and which ones it would be. Because I would presume that he has the capacity to do more than one, and on a good level. So we need to look at this carefully before we decide where he's going.

"We only spoke really with him yesterday in terms of getting to understand him better, what type of rider he really is, from the character perspective, and what he likes, what he doesn't like, and all these things, which are very important when you plan a calendar.

"Now the performance team needs to really take this into consideration and try to set down a draft plan of what it could look like."

While it’s too early to say where Roglič will race, the team have already confirmed a partial plan for their other star signing, Richard Carapaz, who is heading to the Giro d’Italia in May.

Carapaz will certainly race two Grand Tours in 2027 but at this point it has not been confirmed whether that will be the Tour or Vuelta, with that decision again likely to be made after the Vuelta route reveal, and in collaboration with Roglič's schedule.

Carapaz has confirmed his intention to target the GC at the Giro, with Carlstrom indicating he could opt for "differing goals" – ie stage wins – in his second Grand Tour of the year.

Carlstrom insisted the two riders could dovetail well, but Roglič spoke of “sharing the calendar” with his new teammate. That, and given another new climber signing, Santiago Buitrago, is also set for the Giro, would make it unlikely that Roglič heads to Italy in May, even with the draw of the Slovenian stages.

The Tour de France and Vuelta a España, then, would appear to be the logical combination.

items.title: ‘So Stupid’: Mads Pedersen Dumps on One of UCI’s Most Ridiculous Rules
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Cobblestone star blasts regulation that forces riders joining new teams to black out their new bikes before January 1. Better not ask his thoughts about sock height rules, then.
items.lbText:
(Photo: Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

You can always rely on Mads Pedersen to say it how it is.

In his latest quotebomb, the cobblestone bruiser slammed UCI registration rules, deeming them “fucking ridiculous.”

Speaking in this week’s episode of his Lang Distance podcast, Lidl-Trek’s verbose Dane blasted regulation that forces riders moving teams to black out their new equipment until January 1.

“It’s crazy with these contracts, isn’t it? Why don’t they just run from November 1 or December 1?” Pedersen said.

“It’s fucking ridiculous,” Pedersen raged. “It’s so stupid.”

Best not to ask Pedersen’s thoughts about the sock height rules, then.

UCI legislation requires rider contracts to align with the calendar year, rather than the racing season.

That means that riders who hook up with their new teams at December training camps must wear their outgoing employer’s kit. They can ride their new team bikes, as long as they’re debranded.

For example, Primož Roglič was recently spotted at the NSN Cycling winter get-together wearing a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe jersey. The Slovenian was riding what was clearly an NSN-issued Cube bike, albeit with some hastily taped-over logos.

Pedersen suggested to podcast co-host Jakob Egholm that a simple paperwork tweak would fix the farcical off-season ritual.

“The contracts don’t have to be any different,” Pedersen said. “You can just add a clause to the contract saying that if you change teams, you’re allowed to use your new team’s equipment from December 1 or from the first team training camp.

“It would be so easy to change the contracts,” he said. “Then there wouldn’t be any bullshit or riders not getting their salary in December because they’ve ridden a Ridley when they were supposed to ride a Trek.”

Sergio Higuita famously got himself in hot water with EF Education-Nippo at the end of 2021 for this very same “ bullshit.”

The EF team threatened to “fire” the Colombian in the November of his final contract year, and so deny him some salary, after he was seen brazenly pedaling around on a Specialized bike supplied by his new team, Bora-Hansgrohe.

This commotion over contract dates crops up every off-season.

All it takes is a glimpse of a duct-taped bike logo to trigger a rider into a rage.

The continued backlash has prompted the UCI to promise that contract start dates will be officially moved from January 1 to November 1.

UCI director of sport Peter Van den Abeele said at the end of 2025 that such plans are in the works. However, the revised regulation has not yet been implemented.

items.lbText:
Even the best managers can struggle to escape ex-players’ need to manufacture a crisis for content. Enter Michael Carrick …

A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick.

Neville: Just so you know, we’re already filming. This is the intro bit, where we show everyone coming on to set and doing some light banter. It humanises us. The viewer sees it and thinks we’re just mates chatting about football, rather than scions of a global podcast empire commercially obliged to produce an endless scroll of provocative content for money. I always say: why can’t you be both?

Neville: Hang on, these Huel bottles need to be showing the label. Who’s turned the Huels round? Pathetic.

Jamie Carragher enters, followed by Roy Keane and Jill Scott.

Carragher: Salford failed to win at the weekend, Gary!

Neville: Yes, but banal observation about young James at Wigan!

Ian Wright enters, humming a Mary J Blige tune.

Neville: You’re watching Stick To Man United on The Overkill, with ManBank. Look, we all know there are times when you just want to bank with your mates, in a room, together. Download the ManBank app today. We’ve got a special guest today: the former manager of Manchester United Football Club, Michael Carrick. Now Carra, before we start …

Neville: The situation at United right now, it really hurts. I say that as a fan, I don’t use this word lightly, but it’s a real tragedy what’s happened to this football club. OK, you’ve got Grimsby and MK Dons. You’ve got the relegation in 1974. You’ve got Tommy Docherty leaving the club in disgrace. You’ve got Old Trafford being destroyed in a bombing raid during the second world war. You’ve got the very real threat of bankruptcy in the early 1900s. This, to me, is worse than any of that.

Carragher gazing at the ceiling : I always think about the great United teams under Sir Alex. Vidic. Ferdinand. Jaap Stam. Wes Brown. Patrice Evra. Even Denis Irwin, going back to Bruce and Pallister. You had Schmeichel in goal. You had Ince and Bryan Robson in midfield. You had Mark Hughes. You had Cantona. I look at the current side and think: do I see a Mark Hughes in there? Do I see a Cantona? And the answer is: only to an extent .

Neville: Roy, how do United move forward from this? They’ve got Brentford at the weekend.

Keane shrugging : Well, a team like Manchester United, you should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: Yeah, but how do they go about it?

Keane: Well, the players in that dressing room, they need to be looking at themselves. And saying: come on, a team like Manchester United should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: But tactically, what’s the plan?

Keane: If you keep asking me the same question, you’ll get the same answer, only louder.

Scott: I remember something Sarina was telling us at the Euros. We’d just beaten Norway and …

Neville: You take a look at that defence. Yoro. Mazraoui. Dalot. De Ligt. You can’t tell me there’s a worse defence in the history of professional football than those four. You put those four up in a park game, and it would be carnage. You choose any four inanimate objects – say a Kleenex, a butternut squash, a roof tile and a Belkin USB-C to Lightning charging cable – and they would do a better job in defence for Manchester United Football Club.

Carragher: Only thing making it worse is if you and Phil were playing in it!

Wright: Look, I see this United team now, which Roy played in, and Gary played in, and I just think: where’s the heart? Where’s the soul? It’s like they’ve lost something. And until they get it back … I don’t know. I just can’t feel it. I’m not feeling it.

Keane: But you talk about heart, and you talk about soul. These are international footballers ! It’s their job! I’m inexplicably furious about this point in particular!

Carragher: Let’s bring Michael into the discussion here, because you were dealt a tough hand, not just in terms of the recruitment, but the level of scrutiny around the club, around any big club, there’s a noise there. I remember talking to Daniel Agger about it. And Martin Skrtel. Steven Gerrard. Xabi Alonso. Dirk Kuyt.

Scott: There is that constant background chatter, though, isn’t there, at a club like United? I remember Sarina once telling us …

Neville: I remember, the gaffer – Sir Alex – once telling us that at United, a defeat is a disaster. Because of that constant background chatter. Because of how it would be perceived in the media. Did you feel like that constant judgment, whether it was from the media, or from fans, or from prominent ex-players, sometimes on podcasts: did you feel like that was creating extra problems for you?

Twenty-second ad for Manbrella, a precision-engineered umbrella made specifically to fit the male palm. Press Skip to return to video .

Neville: Did you feel like those ex-players in the media, players who had won trophies at United, but who now earn a living off talking about the club, almost preferred it when the club was failing? Because it gave them something to talk about? Because it made their own era look rosy in comparison? Because it did better numbers? And did that broader need to manufacture crisis, to paint every setback as if it was the worst disgrace in human history rather than the inevitable variance of a transitional team in a strong league labouring under an absentee ownership, create an inevitable doom spiral, an inescapable feedback loop from which even the very best managers have struggled to escape over the last 13 years?

Carragher: Sounds like you could be talking about yourself there, Gary!

items.title: Bearman to continue with Haas in 2027
items.content: <article>Britain's Oliver Bearman will continue to race for the Haas team in Formula 1 in 2027.</article>
items.lbText:
Britain's Oliver Bearman will continue to race for the Haas team in Formula 1 in 2027.

The US-based team announced the 21-year-old's new deal on Thursday, at the start of the Qatar Grand Prix weekend.

It marks Bearman's third full season with Haas, for whom he first raced for two one-off events in 2024 before becoming a full-time driver in 2025.

The announcement ends a protracted negotiation period in which Bearman's management were seeking reassurances about his future from Ferrari.

Bearman is a member of the Italian team's driver academy and has ambitions to race for Ferrari in the future.

It was not immediately clear what reassurances Bearman had been given about his future by Ferrari.

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Camara to continue with Haas for final two races

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "Continuing with Ollie into 2027 was a natural decision for us.

"We've seen his growth, his commitment, and the quality he brings to the team, both on and off the track.

"He has a tremendous work ethic and a strong desire to develop both himself and the team, and there is no better person, in my opinion, to lead this team forward."

Bearman added: "It's no secret that I'm delighted to be continuing with Haas into 2027.

"This team has played an integral role in my development, and I've felt a huge amount of belief and support from everyone here.

"We've got big ambitions to keep pushing forward, and I'm excited to lead that work, building on what we've achieved, and striving for even more together – we have unfinished business."

Bearman will be partnered at Haas next season with Brazilian Rafael Camara, who is also a member of the Ferrari driver academy.

Camara has started racing for Haas at the end of this season, following the team's sacking of Frenchman Esteban Ocon midway through the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Bearman's concerns about his future had been rooted in the fact that there might not be a seat available at Ferrari for some considerable time.

Charles Leclerc is on a long-term contract there, and while Lewis Hamilton's deal is believed to end after 2027, the seven-time champion is keen to continue in F1 for a number more years.

Bearman, who said at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, that he was "quite disappointed" his new contract had not yet been sorted so late in the season, is believed to have been exploring his options.

His management is said to have been asking Ferrari for reassurances about his future, either about the possibility of racing for the main team, or if that is not an option, being allowed to pursue a career at a more competitive team than Haas.
