items.title: ‘It’s Not Going to Be Just Sole Leadership’: Quinn Simmons Campaigns for Tour of Flanders
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: After helping Mads Pedersen at the Tour and riding into late-season form, the 25-year-old says Lidl-Trek needs two cards on the table to beat Tadej Pogačar, Mathieu van der Poel, and Wout van Aert.
items.lbText:
Quinn Simmons is angling to ride the Tour of Flanders, the American champion revealed to Velo .

After years of avoiding the cobbled classics, a return to the Belgian monument would be a shake-up for Simmons, who has gravitated towards the hillier monuments in recent years.

It would also be a shake-up for the Lidl-Trek classics squad, with Simmons dropping into a team that has been built around getting Mads Pedersen a monument victory for the better part of the last decade.

It would also be the first time that Simmons has ridden Flanders since his debut in 2022, when he didn’t finish.

“My first objective of the year will be Flanders,” Simmons told Velo in an exclusive interview in Tucson, Arizona. “I still haven’t got the full confirmation that I can go, but in my head that is the first goal.”

The shift in program for Simmons stems from two separate but equally important developments from the 2026 season for the 25-year-old all-rounder.

“When I basically gifted Mads [Pedersen] a Tour stage this year, I think that was when the team started to realize that maybe there’s going to be some changes. For next year, it’s not going to be just sole leadership,” Simmons said.

“If that’s hard for him to accept, that’s how it is. For sure, he’s one of the best riders in the world, but now, with the team we have, we can’t only be putting eight guys around one anymore,” he continued.

“I think it’s not just for myself, but for the other riders we have on the team like [Mathias] Vacek and some other guys coming up. If we go into the monuments, you have to play with two cards. Pogačar, Van der Poel, and Van Aert—they’re too good to only beat with one. We’re gonna need to adapt that plan a bit.”

That confidence was gained not just through the Tour, where Simmons was a frequent attacking and pulling presence, but also through a successful one-day race campaign to end the year.

The high point was the Team USA win at the UCI World Championships with Brandon McNulty, but that was part of a bigger picture where Simmons showed his form throughout the Canadian, Italian, and Japanese races on his program.

He also has Remco Evenepoel as an example of how parachuting into Flanders can fit into a larger calendar.

“It came from how I was racing the one-day races at the end of the year,” Simmons said. “With the way Remco did it, where you do Catalonia first and then go to Flanders, I think it can work. If I can do an altitude block and then come to Flanders quite in good shape.

“If I have to be in Belgium the four weeks before, I just don’t believe I can maintain the form that I need that long, but I think if I can climb with a similar level to Worlds, I believe Flanders has at least the potential for something to happen.”

Simmons began his career as a highly touted classics prospect but quickly moved away from the cobblestones and toward the hill classics and the Tour de France.

While a return won’t change his ultimate goal of a Tour stage win, it does add another chance for Simmons and his Lidl-Trek team to win the big monument they have been lacking.

“If I can be there in the same role there, that’s how Mads [Pedersen] can win—if we go there together,” he said. “Hopefully that gets approved, and if not, then I’ll just do my normal program of going to Basque, Amstel, and then preparing for the Tour.”

items.lbText:
Head coach questions ‘difficult to understand’ decisions

Argentinian offers support to Lammens after errors

Mauricio Pochettino claimed Manchester United were punished unfairly after again appearing to suffer from faulty officiating in Wednesday night’s 2-2 draw at Sporting.

The key decision from Szymon Marciniak came when Amad Diallo’s first-half strike was ruled out due to the referee adjudging Youri Tielemans to have fouled Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish. Tielemans was booked and so when he received a second yellow card in second-half added time, he was sent off for United’s fifth red card in their last nine games. This followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4-0 loss at Liverpool that was later rescinded.

“It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” said Pochettino, who greeted questions about the official’s first caution of Tielemans by saying: “It’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field. Impossible.”

With 10 minutes left United were 2-1 ahead but suffered a chaotic ­ending as Senne Lammens dropped a high cross in front of his goal, allowing Luis Suárez to equalise with a bicycle kick.

Pochettino defended his No 1. “Football is about making mistakes. I want to support always my player. It’s something that happened in that case. We need to talk about responsibility and it’s our responsibility too to provide the best tools,” said the head coach.

“In this type of action also our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult. It’s not to blame the defensive line, but it’s two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. Because sometimes we talk about that professional players need to have refreshed concepts, details until that becomes a habit. And things that we need to improve are habits in a defensive way, offensive way, in all the areas.

“But of course, we need to accept, we accept the challenge and we are here to try to improve, you know, the small details that for sure we will improve.” Lammens saved a first-half penalty from Suárez before conceding another one himself moments later, which the striker coverted.

Bruno Fernandes equalised from the spot on 48 minutes before his bizarre long-range effort – which took a huge deflection off a divot in the pitch – put United ahead.

Despite the chaotic end, Pochettino was impressed by his team. “The structure was really good,” he said. “All the microdoses that we add to the team, I think is helping the structure to be very clear.”

items.title: How the Giro Women Saw Viral Acclaim for Harrowing ‘Elimination of Violence’ Campaign
items.author: Jim Cotton
items.content: Giro d'Italia women's and men's races break the mold by using their sporting platforms to highlight difficult societal issues others might avoid.
items.lbText:
The Giro d’Italia Women and men’s Giro d’Italia blew up Instagram on Wednesday with a post calling out violence against women.

The collaborative post has become one of the most “liked” pieces of content on both profiles and has drawn debate and acclaim across the sport.

The Instagram gallery features a series of juxtaposing images.

The road rash and scuffed knees of racing are paired with harrowing photos of women with black eyes, bloodied knuckles, and bleeding noses.

Each slide features a pair of related captions.

“I slipped – but I know how to get back up” / “I slipped – and I can’t find a way out” is one example.

The final slide and post caption urge better awareness and policing of violence against women.

“No woman should have to hide behind such different stories behind the same words. No woman should ever have to live through something like this,” reads the closing note.

The post Wednesday marked the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women.

November 25 was designated a day to raise awareness that women are subjected to rape, domestic violence, and other forms of abuse by the United Nations General Assembly.

The Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women were among the very few sporting outlets to use their platforms to recognize the campaign.

By contrast, International Women’s Day in March is met annually with (potentially tokenistic) content from stakeholders across world sport.

The Giro d’Italia Women has since been hailed by key figures across professional sport for its proactive, provocative use of its global reach.

Time trial world champion Marlen Reusser, TV pundit and journalist Orla Chennaoui, and the men’s Quick-Step team are among the hundreds to have shown support.

Key figures in athletics, ultramarathon, and Formula 1 also commented.

“It’s so easy for any female brand or gender-neutral brand to jump on a bandwagon when the messaging is convenient,” Chennaoui said in a separate reel commenting on the Giro’s post. “It is so easy to speak up for women on International Women’s Day. In fact, in many cases, it’s detrimental not to.

“Where you see authenticity and where it really matters is when nobody is looking on a random Wednesday morning, and you’re then shouting out in support of and in defense of vulnerable women,” Chennaoui said. “That’s when it matters.”

The Giro d’Italia and Giro d’Italia Women entered a new chapter earlier this year when Luca Guercilena took over as general director of both races.

Guercilena was the long-time general manager of team Lidl-Trek.

The veteran Italian came to his headlining role at RCS Sport this September promising a forward-thinking approach to a very traditional sport.

Guercilena is already hinting at new race dates, formats, and concepts for the historic men’s Giro d’Italia. A progressive approach to social media might be another part of his regimen.

items.title: Knicks 121, Cavs 102: Scenes from a second-half bench bash
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
The Knicks’ hopes of repeating as NBA Cup champions hinged on beating Cleveland (9-10) tonight and Miami on Friday, while Philadelphia had to beat Miami (which they did) and Indiana has to topple Philadelphia. Even then, advancement would come down to point differential, meaning New York (12-6) would likely need to win both games by double digits.

Consider the mission half completed. As you could deduce from the blazing blue court at Madison Square Garden, tonight’s tilt was a Cup game. Three Knicks were sidelined by injury: OG Anunoby, Miles McBride, and Jordan Clarkson. Anunoby’s absence was felt as the Cavaliers scored 61 first-half points (and a lopsided free-throw disparity stung, too). The adjustments Mike Brown made in the locker room paid dividends on the court. His squad applied stingier defense, got their turnovers under control, won the fourth quarter 39-17, and flipped the game to win, 121-102.

Of the six Knicks with double-digit points tonight, Jose Alvarado’s barrage of fourth-quarter triples and his season-high / team-high 21 were arguably the most impactful. On a short-handed night, and with multiple starters playing through injury, Jose was once again prepared to step into the spotlight and contribute meaningful minutes. What a professional! What depth!

Three consecutive turnovers didn’t help (two by Karl-Anthony Towns, one by Josh Hart) as the Knicks fell behind early in the first quarter. Midway through the period, Jalen Brunson scored seven in under two minutes to regain the lead. In this streaky contest, though, it made sense that he missed his next five attempts. Towns (12 PTS, 10 RBS, 7 AST, +21) was a game-time decision due to knee soreness, and his scoring showed the limp, producing a single point in the frame. Filling in for Anunoby in the first five, Landry Shamet made his sixth start of the season. He finished with a tidy 11 points on three made three-pointers.

The quarter was competitive until the final three minutes. After Pacôme Dadiet (yes, him!) drilled a triple to pull the Knicks within one, Cleveland rattled off a 10-0 run, powered by five consecutive points from Meleek Thomas, two Thomas Bryant free throws, and a Donovan Mitchell and-one. The latter easily had the biggest impact on the quarter, tallying 14 points, three dimes, and a steal. As for New York’s bench support, Dadiet (7 PTS, 14 MIN) provided positive defensive efforts with a block and a steal, but neither Tyler Kolek nor Andre Drummond moved the needle. New York managed just six points over the final five-ish minutes, and Cleveland closed the quarter ahead, 34-23.

To start the second, the good guys outscored the villains by ten, chiseling an 11-point deficit to one. Credit Towns and his four points, two dimes, and two blocks for the comeback. Mohamed Diawara lent a triple, too, and Mikal Bridges found his rhythm, blasting out seven fast points. Naturally, Cleveland responded with a 9-2 stretch when James Harden (28 PTS, 1-8 3PT) finally got on the board. Dadiet drizzled water on our good feelings by missing three straight shots, and Brunson still couldn’t regain his touch, going scoreless from the field in the period.

Playing from 55-44 down with four minutes left in the half, the hosts posted 11 unanswered points, eight of which belonged to Bridges. He’d finish the half with 17 points. This, my friends, is what’s known as a :

Despite dealing with a sore shoulder, Hart picked Harden’s pocket twice, converting one steal into a layup. Unfortunately, after Bridges tied the game at 55, Donovan Mitchell (30 PTS, 1-7 3PT) and Harden combined for six unanswered points, aided by a Bridges turnover. The home team won the quarter 33-27 but entered intermission trailing 61-56.

Through the half, Harden and Mitchell combined for 34 points in the half, while their bench contributed 13. New York had shot better from the field (54% to 49%) and significantly better from deep (50% to 31%), they were on the wrong end of the score due to a glaring free-throw disparity. New York had attempted just eight freebies, while Cleveland shot more than twice that. The Cavs outscored won the paint, 28-16, and the boards. Another glaring stat: Cleveland converted six Knicks miscues into 13 points, while New York squeezed just two points out of five giveaways.

Cleveland opened the second half on an 11-5 run to restore its double-digit lead. Down 74-65 midway through the period, the Knicks got a boost from an unexpected source: Tyler Nickel. The rookie sank a triple, followed by another from Landry Shamet, to cut the deficit to three. Nickel contributed five points but also committed four fouls in under six minutes—that will get straightened out with experience. Harden extended Cleveland’s advantage to 85-77 with under three minutes remaining. But then another unexpected player pitched in: James Wiseman provided some valuable minutes off the bench, finishing the game with six points and seven boards in six minutes. Shamet helped the Knicks win the quarter 26-24 and enter the fourth trailing 85-82.

The Knicks opened the fourth quarter on a 12-0 run, turning a three-point deficit into a nine-point advantage in less than three minutes. Jose Alvarado (a team-high 21 points, 8-10 FG, 19 MIN) was the catalyst, drilling consecutive triples and picking Donovan Mitchell’s pocket to set up a Dadiet layup. Hart took a turn orchestrating the offense, collecting four assists during the opening surge. The Ohio Players missed their first five shots, four of them by Mitchell, and committed two turnovers as the Knicks piled on the points.

Wiseman (!) helped goose New York’s lead to 13 with four points and three offensive rebounds in a brief fourth-quarter stint. When Mitchell and Harden scored five unanswered points to trim the deficit to eight, Alvarado responded with a jumper, and Jalen Brunson buried a triple, his only basket of the quarter. Alvarado was the unquestionable star of the fourth, scoring 16 of his 21 points, including four three-pointers. Hart was nearly as impactful, contributing eight points, six assists, three rebounds, a steal, and a block in the frame. The Knicks closed on a 7-0 run, their defense holding Cleveland scoreless over the final two minutes and change.

Welcome back to associate head coach Chris Jent, who returned to the sidelines after a month away.

The Knicks hang around town to face the Heat on Friday in the last of their first-stage Cup games. Mo is folding and pressing your recap. Happy Knicksgiving, turkey fans.

items.title: More ref frustration as Pochettino's chaotic start at Man Utd continues
items.content: <article>What are the findings for Mauricio Pochettino after his first two matches as Manchester United manager?</article>
items.lbText:
Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?

United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.

Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.

This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.

Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".

That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.

Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.

United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.

Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.

A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.

A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.

"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."

Divots, howlers and bad decisions - dissecting Man Utd's draw in Lisbon

Four goals, chaos and controversy - Man Utd held in Lisbon

Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.

The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre.

Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.

Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.

"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.

"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."

United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.

Young said Lammens may be one mistake from being dropped.

The Belgian's performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount.

It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy.

Darlow did end last season as first choice at Leeds but started just 30 league games in his three seasons with the Elland Road club. Tom Heaton, 40, who was also on the bench against Sporting, has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Could Pochettino contemplate leaving Lammens out.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

It has been a whirlwind week for Pochettino, who last Wednesday morning UK time was still United States boss.

There have been a few blows to absorb, and lessons are having to be learned quickly.

But despite the clear frustrations, the 54-year-old is glad he accepted the challenge.

"I am happy to be here," he said. "I'm so excited to be the face representing this club.

"We are here because the situation wasn't the situation all the fans and people expect. We are here to take the responsibility from one week, and we are going to improve for sure.

"It's going to be tough, of course. Nothing is easy. But we have the energy and I think we have the capacity, and, most important, we have the players and the power and the energy from our fans, which is massive."

items.title: Divots, howlers and bad decisions - dissecting Man Utd's draw in Lisbon
items.content: <article>BBC Sport breaks down the chaos amid Manchester United's rollercoaster Champions League draw against Sporting in Lisbon.</article>
items.lbText:
Manchester United were held to a draw in a chaotic and controversial Champions League encounter with Sporting in Lisbon with Mauricio Pochettino denied a first win as United head coach despite his side turning around a first-half deficit.

They were behind at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens conceded from a penalty he gave away – having saved another just minutes before.

United then had a goal disallowed before scoring a penalty of their own through Bruno Fernandes, who then put them in front with the help of a large divot on the pitch.

There was more drama as Lammens dropped the ball for Sporting's equaliser before Pochettino's side had what they thought was a winner ruled out.

Polish referee Szymon Marciniak was at the centre of much of the drama with midfielder Youri Tielemans sent off in stoppage time.

BBC Sport breaks down each incident after a crazy night.

Lammens saved a poor penalty from Sporting's Luis Suarez, given after Lisandro Martinez left a leg out which caught Geny Catamo.

The Belgium keeper got down to hold on to Suarez's low effort which looked set to be a huge boost for the underperforming United number one.

Pochettino's whirlwind week ends with optimism and frustration

Lammens went from hero to zero in the space of 76 seconds as he rushed out of his goal and took out Maxi Araujo in the United box.

Noussair Mazraoui was caught out by a ball over the top but it was reckless from Lammens and this time Suarez buried the spot-kick.

Former United midfielder Owen Hargreaves told TNT Sports: "There is no way Senne Lammens can get there. Just stay in the goal."

Amad Diallo thought he had equalised for United before half-time when he headed in after his first attempted was turned on to the cross bar.

However, referee Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul against Youri Tielemans.

Replays showed Tielemans won the ball and pulled out of the challenge after he played the ball through to Amad.

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson: "Marciniak believed that Goncalo Inacio had been fouled by Youri Tielemens on the edge of the area as the Manchester United midfielder played a pass through.

"Rather than immediately blow his whistle, Marciniak held off to let the move play out.

"But when Diallo hit the bar with his first effort, Marciniak blew his whistle.

"Play was dead at that point, so when Diallo then nodded the rebound over the line the VAR was locked out.

"However, the chances that the VAR would have intervened were very slim.

"Tielemens, who was booked, caught Inacio's foot under his body sliding to make the pass, causing the Sporting defender's ankle to buckle."

Former Manchester United midfielder Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "It's an absolute disgrace. I don't know how the referee is seeing that Tielemans has kicked the player.

"On first viewing, I thought his foot must have hit him on the follow through but when you look at it again, Tielemans actually tries to take his foot away.

"He doesn't touch him because he knows the midfielder is coming towards him.

"It is one of the worst decisions I've seen with a referee giving that decision."

United got back on level terms after a foul on Martinez in the Sporting area by Eduardo Quaresma led to a penalty. Bruno Fernandes converted.

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport: "Martinez wins that penalty, but it is a penalty."

United took the lead with two quick-fire goals but in bizarre circumstances as Fernandes' speculative strike looked like it would be easily collected by Kaique Pereira only to hit a divot on the pitch and fly up past the Sporting goalkeeper.

Former Rangers striker Ally McCoist on TNT Sports: "I think it hits a divot and it jumps over the goalkeeper! That is absolutely incredible."

Hargreaves added on TNT Sports: "Unbelievable. It is like a golf divot. There are holes in this pitch absolutely everywhere.

"Bruno Fernandes created a divot, does he get an assist for that?"

Lammens made another error, spilling a high ball under little pressure from Suarez. The Sporting striker then reacted quickly to find the target with an overhead kick to make it 2-2, the goal given after a quick VAR check.

McCoist: "I am baffled because the forward does what you expect him to do.

"The goalkeeper, instead of concentrating on the ball, he thinks about the player."

United thought they had taken the lead as Sporting keeper Kaique appeared to push the ball into his own net from a Fernandes corner.

However, after a VAR intervention, the 'goal' was then disallowed for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu.

Onuoha: "First that was an absolutely disastrous goal for United to concede for the equaliser. it comes from a nothing ball into the box, too.

"For the United goal that has just been ruled out, the keeper has pushed it into his own net before Dorgu has touched him."

Young added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "The keeper comes out and flaps at it before he is even touched. How that has gone to VAR is beyond me.

"If a referee is on the pitch and being sent to the screen, if he's given the goal then stand by your decision."

Midfielder Tielemans was then sent off for a late challenge on Sergi Altimira. The Belgium international's second yellow compounds the controversial one he received in the first half.

United have now received five red cards in all competitions this season - two more than any other Premier League side.

Young added: "The referee's performance was just simply 'wow'.

"The decisions that he gave. Youri Tielemans getting booked to eventually getting sent off later because you booked him when it should never have been a booking and it should have been an equalising goal.

"His decision-making today is nothing more than a disgrace."

items.lbText:
“We are a strong team,” Mauricio Pochettino exhorted, then watched Manchester United’s unerring ability to cause drama every time they lace up their boots.

Cruising, it seemed, at 2-1 and with 10 minutes left, they unravelled, as Senne Lammens dropped a high ball in front of his goal and a grateful Luis Suárez equalised with a bicycle kick. Cut almost instantly to Sporting’s Kaique Pereira who bundled the ball in for United’s apparent winner only for Szymon Marciniak to be ordered to the screen by the video assistant referee, where the official ruled the goal out for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu.

There was more – of course: Youri Tielemans, in stoppage time, was sent off – this for a second yellow card and United’s fifth red in six weeks. Marciniak issued the first yellow to the Belgian for what looked a non-existent foul that also resulted in Amad Diallo’s perfectly legal strike being chalked off.

The bedlam had also featured United conceding two penalties in two first-half minutes, Lammens saving the first from Suárez, then conceding the second, and being unable to stop the No 9’s second effort.

Marciniak’s questionable display followed Leny Yoro’s red card in Sunday’s 4-0 debacle at Liverpool being rescinded on appeal. Pochettino greeted questions about the official’s first caution of Tielemans with an initial silence but a gesture of his face that showed agreement. Then he said: “It’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field. Impossible.”

Before this United had come from 1-0 behind and were heading for a first victory under Pochettino and only a fourth of this troubled campaign that would have rewarded the 2,597 travelling fans.

But, after the humiliation at Anfield, victory eluded them. Pochettino will have to build from this, his players remain a jumble of disjointedness.

Brentford are up next in Saturday’s first outing in front of the Old Trafford crowd for Pochettino. Keith Andrews is sure to instruct his men to bombard Lammens, whose previous form this term features howlers for two goals in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa earlier this month, plus a mix-up with Lisandro Martínez that allowed Fulham’s goal in their draw in September.

Pochettino preferred to look at the collective regarding Lammens’ drop: “In this type of action also our defensive line needs to cover better the keeper because it was very difficult.”

Pochettino reacted to the Anfield horror-show by dropping Matthijs de Ligt for Harry Maguire, one of four changes that included Joshua Zirkzee starting at centre-forward for the suspended Matheus Cunha.

The Dutchman blasted one chance over – a sign of his less than elite quality. When Pochettino also witnessed Diallo fail to go at his man down the right, Yoro dawdle in the centre circle, and Kobbie Mainoo pass straight to Issa Doumbia, he saw the scale of his task.

Now came serious farce from those in blue. Martínez lost Geny Catamo, scrambled across to challenge, the No 10 went down, and Marciniak awarded the penalty. Suárez hit the spot-kick straight at Lammens: a turning point in United’s horrendous campaign? No.

Moments later Maximiliano Araújo twisted past United’s No 1 and was barged over for the second spot-kick. Lammens was lucky to escape a red card and this time Suárez scored.

Bad luck was next for United. Because when Diallo scored Marciniak blew for the “foul” by Tielemans on Gonçalo Inácio just before the finish, so no video assistant referee enquiry was allowed.

The wider picture, though, concerned Pochettino’s insistence of a lack of fragility. Understandable, as he could not tell reporters otherwise. But, after the PR, came the evidence of another 45 minutes in which his new charges were certainly not robust.

One more mountain to climb, then, in the second half against the 21-time Portuguese champions, who were led by Paulo Fonseca in only a third game in charge since being prised from Lyon for roughly £4.5m compensation.

Five minutes after the break, United pulled ahead. First, a marauding Martínez was fouled by Eduardo Quaresma and Marciniak awarded a third penalty, which Bruno Fernandes converted for the first goal of the Pochettino era. Then, the captain scored a remarkable second.

A speculative left-foot shot from outside the area looked harmless before hitting a divot in front of Pereira, bouncing over the goalkeeper, and in. Fortune, at last, smiled on United and in replays it transpired Fernandes himself had accidentally created the divot just moments earlier.

On 65 minutes Pochettino made a move, as Dorgu and Diogo Dalot came on, Bryan Mbeumo becoming the centre-forward. United were a yard quicker, more streetwise: confidence and belief surging. On 77 minutes Diallo was forced off, Shea Lacey replacing him. But then came the latest chaos to engulf Pochettino’s nascent tenure.

items.title: SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel Reach Agreement—Here Is What It Actually Means
items.author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
items.content: A joint statement closes a 10-day dispute over the GRVL name, with major implications for both the Indigenous-led Arizona ride and SBT GRVL’s trademark defense.
items.lbText:
The controversy around the GRVL trademark has been resolved. Ten days after the issue came to a head, SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel released a joint statement confirming that the Indigenous-led ride can continue to use the GRVL term in its marketing.

The conflict started when Rez Gravel went public with an email the event received from SBT GRVL, notifying it of its trademark of the term GRVL. The post drew widespread attention on social media, with many commenters supporting Rez Gravel and criticizing the GRVL trademark in general.

Now, the dispute is settled. While the full text of the agreement has not been made public, Rez Gravel is permitted to use the GRVL term across its marketing and promotion in perpetuity, with no requirement to change its branding or anything associated with the event going forward.

“SBT GRVL and Rez Gravel are glad to share that we’ve resolved this matter and are moving forward on good terms,” the joint statement read. “After talking things through, both organizations have agreed that Rez Gravel will continue operating under its current name and branding, including REZ GRVL.

“Each organization understands the importance of protecting the brands we’ve built and respects the work the other has put into their respective events. We share a commitment to support the growth of gravel cycling and the communities that make this sport so special.”

In our conversation with SBT GRVL last week, the organization said its intention all along in the email was to reach an understanding with Rez Gravel over the use of the GRVL term. Under U.S. trademark law, trademark holders are required to actively police their marks; allowing unauthorized use to go unchecked can weaken a trademark or render it unenforceable in future disputes. Putting a formal agreement in place satisfies that requirement by establishing that Rez Gravel’s use is explicitly authorized rather than unpoliced.

Following the resolution, Amy M. Charity, founding partner and CEO of SBT GRVL, provided additional comments on the agreement and the event’s position.

“To us, GRVL has always represented so much more than four letters,” Charity said. “It’s about bringing people together, creating welcoming experiences and growing the cycling community. We share many of those same values with Rez Gravel, and we’re genuinely happy to have found a path forward that respects what we’ve each built. We fully support their continued use of GRVL and look forward to seeing their event and community thrive.”

Charity also pointed to SBT GRVL’s size and history with the event. “As a founder of SBT GRVL, this is deeply personal to me,” she said. “We’re a small, four-person business, and we’ve spent the better part of a decade pouring our hearts into creating an experience that people have come to know, love and look forward to year after year. My hope is that something really positive comes out of this and that the cycling community continues to rally around Rez Gravel and support the meaningful work they’re doing.”

Update: Shortly after this story was originally published, Rez Gravel responded to an earlier request for comment from Velo with the following statement:

“Per the agreement with SBT, which I cannot disclose, I’m glad that the matter between the Parties has been resolved, that Rez Gravel continues to use its name and branding, including REZ GRVL, that no money changed hands, and that neither Party admitted any wrongdoing.”

Prior to the joint statement, the organization had indicated that an agreement was in the works, posting on Instagram on November 19 to state its commitment to retaining the GRVL distinction.

Because the agreement grants Rez Gravel perpetual permission to use the mark—and formally documents that consent—the arrangement settles the question for future editions of the Arizona ride while keeping SBT GRVL’s broader trademark defense intact.

items.title: Williams exceeded F1 cost cap by £627,000
items.content: <article>Williams "unintentially" broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA finds.</article>
items.lbText:
Williams broke Formula 1's cost cap during the 2025 season, governing body the FIA has found.

The team say they "unintentionally" exceeded the cap by £627,000. Last season, the spending limit was $135m (£106m).

Alpine were also found to have broken the rules, although theirs was a procedural breach without overspending.

Both teams have reached so-called 'accepted breach agreements' with the FIA.

Williams' involves a financial penalty, the amount of which has not been disclosed, and a 1.5% reduction in permitted aerodynamic research and development time for the next 12 months.

Alpine have also been given an undisclosed financial penalty.

Both teams must foot the costs of the investigations by the FIA into their rule-breaking.

A Williams statement said: "The breach relates to administrative costs we incurred making changes to our company structure.

"We believed these costs fell outside of the cap. Following discussions with the FIA, we have agreed to resolve the matter in line with their interpretation that the costs should have been in cap.

"The FIA has noted that Williams did not gain any sporting or financial advantage, and nor did we ever seek to. It has also noted that we acted co-operatively and in good faith throughout the review process.

"Integrity is central to what Williams stands for and we can now close this case and remain focused on our future."

The FIA said in a statement: "There is no accusation or evidence that (Williams) sought at any time to act in bad faith, dishonestly or in a fraudulent manner, nor that it wilfully concealed any information from the cost-cap administration.

"The financial regulations are complex, and the breaches arose from an interpretation adopted by (Williams) in good faith.

"Williams has accepted the FIA's interpretation and the resulting breaches."

It said Williams' breach was the equivalent of a 0.48% overspend, which "falls at the lower end of the less than 5% minor overspend range".

Williams' costs were incurred as the team tried to update their operations in order to become more competitive.

Williams had targeted the new 2026 regulations as an opportunity to make a significant step forwards in the team's attempt to return to the front of F1.

Instead, the team have taken a step backwards, and after finishing fifth in 2025, are lying ninth in the constructors' championship with two races remaining this season.

Alpine said in a statement: "The team accepts that it unknowingly committed a procedural breach, which is a result of inaccuracies in the full-year reporting documentation for costs related to exclusions and adjustments.

"The errors and inaccuracies in the reporting were specifically related to non-sporting and operational costs which the CCA recognised didn't give the team any performance advantage, such as marketing activities, non-F1 activities, HR activities, employees' bonus costs, offsetting of costs, and costs of inventories."

'The more I was thinking, the more I didn't know what to do' – Primož Roglič on looking retirement in the eye, his 'really fast' move to NSN, and why he could even race beyond 2027
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
Primož Roglič looked retirement square in the eye this off-season. He didn’t mind what he saw, but there was a definite itch as he pictured his career in that hypothetical rear-view mirror.

"You have two sides," he explained, speaking at his new team's first pre-season training camp. "If you want to finish when you can choose, you want to finish while you are still good, or on the top.

"The other is that I'm still attracted by cycling, you know. I like it. I like to compete, I still have unfinished businesses with it... [so that] I can peacefully say at the end of my cycling career that that was it."

Roglič went on to describe the sort of situation in which it would make no sense for him to carry on: "That you don't care, if it's first place, 10th place, 100th place – just that it doesn't touch you anymore and you are done with it."

That’s clearly not the case for the 37-year-old champion of five Grand Tours. And not just that, but 2027 is not necessarily the end, either.

Roglič’s has joined NSN on a one-year contract that was billed by the team themselves as 'the final chapter'. However, he is not ruling out continuing his career into 2028.

"You know, how to say it… the only fixed thing in life…" he said, perhaps referring to the saying that the only two certainties in life are death and taxes.

"We start with this one [season]. In the minute it’s the final one, but let’s start and we see how we go, and where we go."

Roglič was then asked about the possible Tour de France Grand Départ in his native Slovenia in 2029.

"Now it’s 2027. In 2029 I will be 40," he joked. He did go on to say "maybe", but, as the journalist in question revealed he himself was 40, he was clearly in tongue-in-cheek mode: "Ah you look good. Yeah, Maybe, maybe, if I look like this, then yeah."

Roglič’s move to NSN, announced last Wednesday, was a sudden and surprising end to a transfer saga that had rumbled on for much of the season.

It was clear by the summer that the four-time Vuelta a España winner would not be continuing at Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, and he didn’t appear to be awash with options, with Lotto-Intermarché, Tudor Pro Cycling and Pinarello-Q36.5 being the strongest links.

The uncertainty rumbled on right through to his last race of the season, Il Lombardia, where he told us he might just be about to race his final race. He had offers on the table but he had a more pressing concern: whether or not he even wanted to carry on.

"It took a while, definitely, for me to figure it out, after the season – what to do, in which direction to go," Roglič said.

"Then I started thinking, and the more I was thinking, the more I didn't know actually what to do.

"So in the end, I really needed to let it go, you know, to look from a bit of a different perspective at some things."

Roglič stated that the fundamental decision over retirement came first, and then made way for the more practical considerations of what another season could look like.

"First of all, it was more about continuing racing or not. And yes, then, okay, this was done. But then still it was open – how to continue, where to continue.

"When I'd figured it out, I mean, what actually would count the most for me? What would be something new, something different?

"In the end, I came to the things, or the basics, that I would appreciate the most. So that was trust, belief, and support from the team and all the rest around the equipment and whatever that follows into this."

A lightning fast move to NSN

Roglič firmly felt he found those things with NSN Cycling, the team formerly known as Israel-Premier Tech that in 2026 turned into the Swiss-registered outfit that’s now operated by ex-footballer Andres Iniesta’s ‘Never Say Never’ company.

NSN, who had little in the way of climbing or GC depth but now have Roglič and Richard Carapaz on the books, weren’t in the mix until very recently. In fact, Roglič had solid offers in his hand at the time he was mulling his retirement, but contact with NSN only came very late, and accelerated very quickly.

It was less than two weeks ago, he says, that he and his agent sat down with the team’s representatives, including general manager Kjell Carlstrom, sporting manager Steve Bauer, and head sports director Sam Bewley.

"I mean, first of all, they listened, you know, they listened," Roglič said pointedly.

"And when they spoke, I got the feeling that they are the ones that I can get full trust in, that I will get full support and belief. So with that kind of feelings, it was pretty fast."

A few days later, he had put pen to paper, and a few days after that, he arrived in south east Spain at the team’s first pre-season training camp. And a few days on again, he's talking to us.

"It was really fast and easy, and I'm happy that I got this opportunity, and I'm really happy that I'm here now," Roglič said.

"Let's say I didn't care, and I started to discover… I started to, yeah, to be actually positively surprised since I came last Saturday here to the team camp."

Roglič did not map out his 2027 calendar, saying that all three Grand Tours were enticing in their own way but that it was “too early” to be thinking about that, adding: "it’s unfair now to do this, because now I try to meet here 150 people, I don’t know much about the equipment. First things first."

More generally, though, he knows he has to take care of that unfinished business. This autumn he came agonisingly close to an outright-record fifth Vuelta title, and went on to win the European time trial title.

They wouldn't have been a shabby set of results to bow out on, and they would in fact take some beating in 2027, but it's more the idea of going out on his own terms.

"I hope something good," Roglič said of what he hopes to get out of 2027. "Everyone likes things to happen, if you say victories or whatever, but the only sure thing is challenges. The challenges will come. You know, the shit things will come. That is something that is pretty sure, and that actually I'm looking forward to – to dealing with it.

"Hopefully I still can give, in terms of results, definitely something good back, and that we are all happy, you know, with giving our best this year."

items.title: Confusion and anger - Yoro red card rescinded, but row goes on
items.content: <article>Leny Yoro's red card against Liverpool has prompted an unseemly difference of opinion between Man Utd and Pro Ref.</article>
items.lbText:
Leny Yoro's overturned red card against Liverpool appears to have turned into an unseemly difference of opinion between Manchester United and referees' body Pro Ref.

Yoro was sent off after bringing down Liverpool striker Alexander Isak in the eighth minute of the 4-0 defeat at Anfield.

Referee Sam Barrott sent off the France international, and the decision was backed up by video assistant referee (VAR) John Brooks.

It split opinion among pundits and fans. Would Isak have got to the ball before goalkeeper Senne Lammens? Was it really a clear goalscoring chance?

First, a Football Association regulatory commission upheld United's appeal and cancelled the red card.

Then Pro Ref boss Howard Webb said the red card was not "clearly wrong" - just moments before United held a pre-match news conference.

Over to Red Devils head coach Mauricio Pochettino, who was fiercely critical of the decision, and in particular the VAR.

But how can Pro Ref still believe the decision was right when an FA commission said it was wrong?

BBC Sport looks at how the system works.

So United won their appeal. Pro Ref would disagree. Could the two sides not just agree to differ?

"You ask me a question and I need to defend our situation and our club and our players," Pochettino said about Yoro's red card.

It continued a theme from his post-match news conference.

You can see why Pochettino would be keen to talk about the red card, rather than the performance of his players. After all, United had just lost the first game of his tenure. Was the Argentine keen to create a siege mentality?

You can also understand United's frustration - two of their biggest games of the season so far have been defined by refereeing decisions.

The first was the VAR error to allow Erling Haaland's match-winning goal in the Manchester derby, when Enzo Fernandez clearly committed an offside offence.

As for the Yoro incident, Pochettino reserved much his criticism for the VAR. United felt he only took a cursory look at where the ball would run.

It should be noted that Match Officials Mic'd up, on which Webb gave his views, was filmed on Monday evening - before the result of the appeal.

Would that change his opinion? Almost certainly not.

Webb acknowledged the argument against a red card, which was Isak would not get the ball. But he was adamant it was not such an egregious error that it required a VAR intervention.

So are we back to arguing about when VAR should get involved?

The VAR threshold is too high, until it is too low. Rinse and repeat.

It is the Premier League clubs, and not Pro Ref nor the FA, who set where the bar sits.

Take the last stakeholders' survey, which helps to shape how the game is officiated.

It found 65% wanted to maintain the current threshold for VAR intervention, 20% to increase it, and just 15% to lower it.

But, of course, where the Yoro incident sits is still a matter of opinion.

How confusing it must be for a supporter just watching on, hoping to understand.

An FA regulatory commission has said the red card decision was wrong. Case closed? Not so fast.

Pro Ref will not always agree with the decision of an appeal board, nor will they use it as a barometer for future decisions.

And the burden of proof for a VAR intervention is considered higher than for an FA commission.

Pro Ref places far more stock upon the judgements of the Premier League's Key Match Incidents Panel.

The KMI Panel creates the merit table for referees, and helps shape how decisions are made in the future - especially for the VARs.

But surely the FA is the higher body? Not quite.

The FA is responsible purely for disciplinary measures and has no say on how games at the professional level are refereed.

If the Premier League tells Pro Ref the decision is right or wrong, that counts far more than any vote by an FA commission.

BBC Sport understands the club argued that if Isak had maintained his top recorded speed, he would not have got to the ball first.

The club say that is objectively provable, within minutes, using data. This, they say, was not a subjective decision.

To argue it was not subjective goes completely against the nature of the decision - it required a referee's judgement.

Whatever this data was, it most definitely was not available to the referees. The VAR cannot call upon a 3D animation of each player, detailing their running speed and providing an objective result.

How much stock did the commission place on this evidence? We will not know until the written reasons are published in a few days' time.

But United are not going to let this lie, and Pro Ref is not going to bend.

Such is the way FA commissions work, you can never be sure who will win.

There are three panel members who are usually former players, but occasionally you might get a retired referee.

The role of the commission is not to "usurp the referee by re-refereeing the incident".

A designated referee delegate is present to answer questions on the laws of the game, but they cannot offer an opinion on the incident.

The only input Pro Ref has is the official's report - a short entry by the referee that says which law was used for the red card. There is no other context.

It will read something like this: "I have to report that I, as the referee, sent off Yoro, Leny of Manchester United FC Under Law 12 section: S5."

The burden is on the club to prove its case by submitting a body of evidence - videos, images and testimony.

There is no right of reply. The evidence is weighed up by the panel, a vote is cast and the majority wins.

It makes predicting the outcome notoriously difficult, as the system is an opinion poll based upon a club trying to persuade at least two people to agree with them.

Take a look at Aston Villa 's successful appeal against Douglas Luiz's red card for violent conduct four years ago. Luiz had been sent off via a VAR review for a headbutt on Aleksandar Mitrovic.…

items.title: Get big savings on the best waterproof winter cycling gloves we've tested in this Black Friday deal
items.author: Rich Owen

Winter is just starting to show its teeth with falling temperatures and icy winds kicking in. Your hands are on the frozen front line when it comes to cold weather riding, so it's well worth investing in a decent pair of winter gloves to keep your fingers nice and toasty.

items.title: Landry Shamet has arrived. Why can’t he be Sixth Man of the Year?
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Chicken Littles can relax. Our world champion Knicks are 11–6, sit fourth in the Eastern Conference, and have won eight of their last 10 games, including five straight. Karl-Anthony Towns is having an MVP-caliber season, and Captain Jalen Brunson is warming up after a short, celebration-heavy offseason. Another player who’s getting some buzz isn’t one of the starters, but the team’s sharpest weapon off the bench.

When asked about Landry Shamet’s play this season, head coach Mike Brown said the 6’5” guard “should be Sixth Man of the Year. It’s not close.” Mike should know. He has a front-row seat to the Shamet show every night and at every practice.

One stat I take note of is Game Score. John Hollinger designed it to measure a player’s box-score production in a single game. Game Score uses a scale that roughly resembles points scored, with 10 considered an average performance and 40 an outstanding one. It rewards scoring, made field goals, rebounds, assists, steals, and blocks. Shot attempts, missed free throws, turnovers, and personal fouls subtract from the total, and offensive rebounds count more than defensive rebounds.

Through 17 games, Shamet has averaged a Game Score of 8.24. That puts him fourth on the team behind Towns (19.83), Brunson (18.66), and OG Anunoby (11.57). Two starters, Josh Hart and Mikal Bridges, rank fifth and sixth at 6.35 and 5.94, respectively.

This season has been a coming out party for Landry. Although primarily a linchpin of the second unit, he has filled in for starters five times this campaign and is averaging 26.9 minutes per game, the second-most of his NBA career. Consider these statistics, all career-best:

  • A shade under 50% from the field
  • 65% effective field goal percentage
  • Eight field goal attempts per game
  • 5.6 triples tried per game
  • 11.4 points per game, fourth-best on the team

The only Knick shooting better from deep is Jordan Clarkson (50%), coincidentally the 2020–21 Sixth Man of the Year. And Jordan’s attempted only 12 longballs.

When Hart and Bridges have struggled to find the net, plenty of people have beaten the drum for Shamet to replace one of them in the first five. That sounds fine in theory, but consider Mike Brown’s perspective. First, there’s the harmony of keeping the Villanova brethren together, and who knows what effect a “demotion” for Josh or Kal might have on the locker room? Second, Shamet is Mike’s security blanket. If the starters are spinning their wheels, nothing injects energy into the festivities like a Landry pull-up three on the move. The MSG crowd explodes, and you can see his teammates quicken with excitement. Furthermore, Shamet is doing much of his damage against the opponent’s backups. That’s hardly a fair fight. AND when the score is close and the team needs a bucket, Brown can turn to Captain Clutch, Towns, and his sparkplug Shamet. Even if Landry doesn’t start, he sure can finish.

One downer about Landry’s success is the ripple effect on the roster. Overshadowed by Shamet’s sizzling shooting is the fact that Miles McBride is also shooting a career high from downtown (42%). Deuce was once a first-off-the-bench candidate. Now, with Shamet hitting the three-ball and Tyler Kolek coming into his own as a playmaker (averaging 4.1 assists to 0.6 turnovers in 13.3 minutes per game), McBride is down to 17.2 minutes per night, the fourth-highest average of his six-season career. Meanwhile, the Knicks find themselves dreadfully thin at center, with Andre Drummond losing the plot around the 10-minute mark most nights and James Wiseman yet to prove he can hang. Shamet + Kolek + Drummond + Wiseman = an expendable Deuce. No one here will be surprised if McBride, the longest-tenured Knick, is traded before the deadline for a serviceable big man. No, we won’t like it, but we’ll understand it.

Consider this: only three Knicks have won Sixth Man of the Year.

    Why can’t ShamWow be the fourth? He’ll have some stiff competition in the race. Boston’s Payton Pritchard is the current betting favorite for Sixth Man of the Year (+160 at BetMGM). That vanilla Milk Dud averages 13.7 points per game. Other top contenders include Ajay Mitchell (Thunder), Dylan Harper (Spurs), Jrue Holiday (Blazers), and Ayo Dosunmu (Timberwolves). Jared McCain and Daniss Jenkins are dark horses.

    The stats make Landry a strong candidate, though. Through Nov. 22, Shamet ranked fifth in the NBA in on/off net rating among 242 qualifying players on HoopsNightly’s leaderboard. The Knicks outscored opponents by 17.2 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and were outscored by 8.3 with him off it. That’s a swing of +25.5. (KnickStats gives him an even better number, +28.)

    There used to be two knocks on Shamet, now in his ninth season. The first was that his defense stunk. Well, whattayaknow: according to KnickStats, the Knicks have allowed 101.3 points per 100 possessions with him on the floor and 117.5 with him off it. The other concern was the injury bug. He’s missed significant time with lower-body issues, including multiple ankle sprains, a foot injury that kept him out for an extended stretch in 2023, and a calf strain that ended his 2023–24 season. Then came the right-shoulder setbacks, a dislocation in the 2024 preseason and a sprain in 2025 that sidelined him for roughly a month. For now (no jinxes), he’s been the picture of health, playing every game of the campaign (we all wince whenever he smashes to the floor).

    Everything’s good until it isn’t again. So it goes. For now, the Knicks are surging and tonight they’ll face a familiar rival in the Cleveland Cavaliers. If you saw the injury report, it’s a little dicey. Anunoby and Clarkson are out, while Hart, McBride, and Towns are all game-time decisions. That’s a concerning list at first blush, but with sixth man Shamet in their back pocket, the Knicks still have a good chance to win their sixth straight. What a time to be a fan.

items.title: How Primož Roglič Went From the Brink of Retirement to Signing With NSN in Days
items.author: ahood
items.content: Primož Roglič was a lot closer to retirement than everyone thought: How weeks of soul-searching and one decisive meeting sealed the deal within days.
items.lbText:
Roglič agonized over his decision whether to retire or not. (Photo: Gruber Images)

Primož Roglič spent weeks agonizing over whether to retire before needing just a few days to hammer out a deal to join NSN Cycling .

Roglič was off-contract with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe this year, and despite a slew of rumors that he was talking with other teams, just a few weeks ago, he still didn’t know if he’d be racing in 2027.

Speaking from his new team’s training camp in Spain, the 37-year-old admitted the biggest decision wasn’t which team to race for in 2027, but whether to race at all.

“Obviously, it took a while. It took a while definitely for me to figure it out, and then after the season, what to do, in which direction to go,” Roglič said on a call Wednesday.

“And the thing was that, the more I was thinking, the more I didn’t know actually what to do. So at the end, I really needed to let it go to look from a bit of a different perspective at some things.”

After reports of several deals falling through , Roglič revealed coming into November, he still didn’t know if he’d be racing.

But once NSN reached out, things moved quickly.

Roglič met with NSN’s manager Kjell Carlström, coach Paulo Saldanha, and sport director Steve Bauer less than two weeks ago, and within days, one of the biggest surprise transfers of the winter was sealed.

“And when I come in touch with NSN, I had a meeting with a couple of guys. Then it went super fast,” Roglič said. “Then in a couple of days, we signed because I get the belief and trust of the people, support, and, yeah, that was it, and that was enough.

“And the name itself, ‘Never Say Never,’ helped even more. So, yeah, three days later I was here in a team camp.”

It’s the latest twist in Roglič’s unique and sometimes unconventional pro racing career.

A former ski jumper, he didn’t turn pro on the road until mid-20s. Just when it looked like he was poised to rule the Tour de France, Tadej Pogačar shows up.

After three years with Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, when he won a record-tying fourth Vuelta a España, the arrival of Remco Evenepoel meant he was the odd man out.

Roglič was overlooked for the Tour de France, so he wanted to go out with a bang. But then disaster struck just weeks before the Vuelta a España.

“I was hit by a car and I was not sure of going to Vuelta. I went all in to make myself ready. I was there. Then I want to win,” Roglič said. “I still got some good results toward the end of the season.”

Roglič was torn from walking away from cycling while he was still capable of winning at the highest level. Second at the Vuelta and a win at the European time trial championships proved he’s still near the sharp end of the peloton.

But he said he still loved the thrill of racing.

Roglič agonized day and night trying to decide if he wanted another season in the WorldTour.

“There are two sides,” he said. “You want to finish when you choose and when you’re on top. On the other, I’m still attracted to cycling. I like to compete.”

So what did NSN offer Roglič that convinced him to sign on the dotted line?

“And at the end, it came to the things or the basics that I would appreciate the most,” he said. “A trust, belief and support from the team.”

There are unconfirmed reports that Roglič took a haircut on his salary, but NSN Cycling did not reveal financial terms of the one-year deal.

Roglič’s late-hour arrival at NSN’s winter camp means no one yet has a clear idea of what his 2027 racing calendar might look like.

The Giro d’Italia’s proximity to Slovenia appeals to him, but so does a return to the Tour after missing out in 2026. And there’s always the prospect of another crack at the Vuelta.

“First things first,” Roglič said. “I need to get to know 150 people, learn the bikes, the equipment. Then we’ll start to make a more detailed program.”

NSN brass will be hoping to squeeze out one good season from Roglič’s legs as the team needs a strong 2027 to solidify the team’s ranking going into the next three-year WorldTour cycle. It ended 2026 ranked 19th, one spot out of the WorldTour guarantee.

One unexpected bonus of the move is teaming up with longtime grand tour rival Richard Carapaz, part of an ambitious transfer class that also includes Santiago Buitrago, American Artem Schmit, and Lennert Van Eetvelt.

“I’m especially happy to be in the same team because we were racing against each other our whole life,” Roglič said. “I’m his fan. I like the way he races, the way he deals with some things or the way he’s doing it. I mean it will be even nicer if we can achieve some good results together for this team.”

And will 2027 be the final act of the Primož Roglič show?

“We start with this one,” he said. “Let’s start and we see how we go and where we go.”

items.title: Injured Bagnaia will miss last GP with Ducati, first MotoGP test with Aprilia
The UCI's registration rules strike again, delaying Shirin van Anrooij's debut with Canyon-SRAM
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
Now, the Dutch rider will have to don a plain jersey for the first five weeks of her off-road season, Canyon-SRAM announced on Instagram.

"Since joining Canyon-SRAM on Nov. 1, @shirnivananrooij has settled nicely into the team & familiarised herself with new equipment. In accordance with UCI regulations, she'll be registered independently & compete in non-team kit for cyclo-cross races from Nov. 27 until Jan. 1," the team wrote.

Van Anrooij is due to race alongside new teammate Zoe Backstedt in the first round of the UCI World Cup in Ostrava on Friday and another dozen races, culminating with the UCI Cyclo-cross World Championships at the end of January.

However, because her transfer from Lidl-Trek to Canyon-SRAM was not completed in the UCI's mid-season transfer window of August 1-15, her registration with her new team cannot officially take effect until January 1.

Van Anrooij could have been racing in the Canyon-SRAM kit had the team registered a cyclo-cross team separately. Blanka Vas will be racing cyclocross with Lidl-Trek after leaving SD Worx-ProTime.

Registration rules have long plagued professional cycling, resulting in incoming riders being put in the awkward position of wearing plain kits during teams' December training camps, and hiding photo shoots in their new kit under lock and key until the dawn of the new year.

Knicks Bulletin: ‘No excuses’
items.author: Antonio Losada
items.content:
Isn’t it crazy that nearly a fifth of the Knicks’ regular-season games after tonight’s matchup would have been played against the same opponent in the Cavs?

Well, that’s true, and so is that New York is about to beat Cleveland to take a 2-1 series lead, won’t it?

Here’s a damn whole lot of quotes to keep you entertained before tipoff.

On the inconsistency of the media’s coverage and criticism of Mikal Bridges:

“Yes. Yes. But that’s your guys’ [the media] job; that’s why you guys get paid. You guys get paid to question and embellish and some other things. We understand that; we know it. You’re looking for stories; we know it.”

On Cleveland’s physicality and what the Knicks must improve in their third meeting Wednesday:

“They were real physical in Game 2. You give them credit. They talked about keeping us off the glass and some other things, and they did it. They’re a great-coached team with Kenny Atkinson and a great team in general.

“There’s gonna have to be a lot of things that we do better in this game, starting with the level of physicality, while getting out in transition, if we expect to get a win.”

On using Jose Alvarado alongside Jalen Brunson to relieve defensive pressure:

“To be able to get (Brunson) off the ball and let somebody else handle the pressure has been huge for us. And also, it gives (Brunson’s) defender a different rhythm, as opposed to being on the ball from the start to the end. You can get in a certain rhythm and get locked in pretty good with it. It can be to your advantage, but if he’s on the ball, then off the ball, then back on the ball, that’s a little harder to adjust to.”

On drawing inspiration from how Golden State deployed Stephen Curry:

“I’m not comparing the players at all in terms of their game, but when I was in Golden State, we used Steph (Curry this way). He was on the ball, then he was off the ball, and to have to make that adjustment throughout the course of the game, not just once or twice but multiple times, is huge. And Jose gives us that ability, because he can guard certain players on the other team, and then if you wanna pressure him, he’s been in that position before. He’ll go by you and sometimes still execute our offense, but he can go by you and make you pay with sprays.”

On his preseason conversation with Jose Alvarado and Tyler Kolek about competing for minutes:

“I said, ‘Hey, right now, Jose, it’s your job because you finished the season that way and you both helped us win at a high level.’ ‘Tyler, you helped us win the NBA Cup and Jose, you helped us win in the finals.’ And I said you guys are really close and it may be you, Jose, for seven games and then it could be Tyler for three, so it’s going to be a competition you have to be ready for the entire year.”

On Alvarado’s defensive advantages over Kolek and the latter’s development:

“Jose Alvarado gives us that ability because he can guard certain players on the other team. And then if you want to pressure him he’s been in that position before, he’ll go by you and sometimes still execute our offense, but he can go by you and make you pay with sprays.

“Tyler Kolek has been getting better on the defensive end of the floor. He’s improved a lot and he’s going to continue to improve as a young guy but Jose has been in the league longer and he knows the league, a little quicker. Teams don’t try and attack him in an iso situation because, as quick as he is, if you mess around with the ball too much he may get a steal and go the other way with it.”

On the Alvarado-Brunson pairing not being exclusively reserved for closing games:

“Well it’s not closing moments. It’s just throughout the course of the ballgame, it’s slotted on my minute sheet and if you think back, the probably best game that comes to mind is in Indiana. Even in the first [of two games last week] in Toronto teams are picking up trying to wear him down and so to be able to get him off the ball and let somebody else handle pressure has been huge for us.

“Also, it gives his defender a different rhythm as opposed to being on the ball from the start to the end. You can get in a certain rhythm and get locked in pretty good with it and it can be to your advantage but if he’s on the ball then off the ball then back on the ball that’s a little harder to adjust to.”

On Josh Hart’s triple-double and defensive performance against Indiana:

“Josh, triple-double. He was really good tonight on both ends of the floor. He was our defensive player of the game, so just a whale of a game for him.”

On Landry Shamet’s season to date:

“He should be sixth man of the year. It’s not even close.”

On identifying with Knicks fans:

“I always see myself in the fans. I look in the crowd, and I see 19,000 people that look just like me.”

On Knicks fans pulling over on the highway in the Hamptons to take pictures with him:

“I was just with my family. I forgot what we were doing. We were doing something and it was, like, three, four or five cars that’s driving, pulling over to ask for photos. I’m like, bro, I ain’t one of these [superstars]. I ain’t KD. I ain’t Bron. I ain’t Steph. But for that it was funny because I’m just like, that shows you the love and the appreciation that New York Knicks fans have, to be on the highway and pull over and ask me for a photo. Whether you’re in New York, the Hamptons or any vacation spot that real New Yorkers go to, you get the love and the appreciation. It’s cool because you’re able to see what the actual heartbeat of the Garden is.”

On the image that comes to mind when thinking about hardworking New Yorkers:

On seeing his own sacrifices and work ethic reflected in Knicks fans:

“When people ask me about it, I always say I see myself in the fans because at the end of the day, well, yeah, I’m probably a little more athletic than they are, a little more gifted in terms of basketball than they are, but New York is hard work. It’s a lot of countless hours, a lot of loss, you know, losing sleep, a lot of sacrifice. And I feel like it’s the same in my shoes, and that’s when I go out and play as hard as I can, because I look in the crowd and I see 19,000 people that look just like me. I think that’s what New Yorkers look like.”

On finding consistency in New York under Tom Thibodeau:

“I felt like I had moments in L.A. and New Orleans and Portland. But I feel like once I got to New York, starting with Thibs, it was a constant.”

On his unpredictable playing style and approaching NBA games like playground basketball:

“I feel like sometimes that’s why a scouting report might be tough for someone like me because it’s just, like, you don’t know what he’s gonna do this day. You don’t know if he might hit four or five threes today or he might have 2 points but 15 rebounds or he might have 6, 7 assists. If you go to a park right now and you just see a kid playing and just doing random stuff, that’s JHart, and that’s how I look at it when I step on the court. I look back to when I’m playing in the playground, I’m just doing random stuff. But it’s random stuff within somewhat of a structure.”

On prioritizing his teammates’ success over his own:

“I don’t really play the game for praise or anything like that. I’ll leave that. I want JB to get his flowers, KAT, Kal, OG, Deuce, Lan. I want those guys to get their flowers, and if I get it, cool. But that’s more important to me, seeing those guys get the accolades that they want, the contracts that they want, the money that they want, the notoriety that they want. And if they get that and I don’t get any, I’m cool with it. So I don’t know, I just… I feel like it changed. I feel like before, you know, you wanted the glitz and the glamour about it, but I don’t know. It’s not really in my heart anymore.”

On unrealistic expectations surrounding Bridges because of the Knicks’ trade package:

“Everyone looks at the trade package and they expect him to be like a No. 2 guy, No. 3 guy, but that’s not what is asked of him to do. He was a guy who was the No. 1 option in Brooklyn. I’m not sure what it was, but I’m sure he was probably averaging around 20 [points per game] or close to it. We got him and we basically asked him to take a smaller role. So you’re not necessarily gonna get the production of a 1A guy being the fourth option, the fifth option at times.”

On Bridges sacrificing individual production for the team’s success:

“I think it’s unfair in that regard, because he could do more, and I’m sure at times he wants to do more, but he’s willing to sacrifice and put the team in front of himself, which we commend him for. … His role could be bigger. I’m sure he at times would like it to be bigger. But he never says anything about it, he never mopes around about it. He just does what is asked of him to do and he tries to do it to the best of his ability.”

On passing up easy baskets to give others scoring opportunities:

“I don’t play the game for stats. I just saw an open man in front of me. Kind of the same thing in Toronto where it was a bobbled play; I could have went and got a dunk and tried to get going offensively. But see a guy in front of me, I’m going to pass it.”

On Brunson returning a pass to help him overcome his physical and mental struggles during recent games

“Oh yeah, for sure. That shows, obviously, he knows I’ve been struggling a little bit physically and mentally and trying to figure it out and trying to get there, that was one of the things, get that pass, get an easy two points, see the ball go through and then play.”

On climbing the Knicks’ all-time triple-double leaderboard and late improvement:

“I don’t know. It feels good to be stacking up some good games. I feel like the last couple games have been better. I have been knocking down shots, but the quality of my play has been better. Obviously, it feels good to have three games in a row that have been better. It feels good that I continue to stack them.”

On dealing with a lingering injury to his shooting shoulder:

“A lot of things are going on with my shoulder. It’s been barking for a couple weeks. So now, we got a couple days where we can figure some stuff out within the couple-day break and hopefully get it feeling better.”

On whether his shoulder injury is affecting his shooting:

On whether Taylor Swift is welcome at Madison Square Garden:

“Obviously. I can’t believe I have to say this. But I didn’t say what was said. Being one of the leaders of the team — the captain of the team — I guess I now have to help somebody out. Yes, she’s a member of the Knicks fandom. Yes, she is.”

On outside narratives surrounding Bridges and his work ethic:

“Everyone outside this organization has their own narrative or belief in things that we can do as a team or players can do individually. But that’s just their own narrative. … He’s one of the hardest workers we have and that won’t change.”

On Bridges’ ability to deliver in high-pressure situations:

“We’ve seen what he does when the lights are the brightest. He steps up to the plate. Mikal’s one of those guys, when you have him in the locker room, when he’s on your team, you feel really good about your odds.”

On what makes Alvarado such a difficult opponent:

“It’s annoying. Any person on the other team will tell you the same thing. He’s a pest. Obviously, you see him shooting the ball really well these last two games. When he’s bringing his whole arsenal to the game, he’s a dangerous player for any team.”

On Bridges’ character, work ethic and ability to handle outside criticism:

“He’s one of the best people I know. I get the pleasure of seeing him every day and seeing how he works. Knowing that any good and bad stretch in the NBA can change very quickly, he’s always in a position to put himself in a good position and keep himself there. He knows what he’s capable of, I know what he’s capable of, and he’s always gonna do the right thing, take care of his teammates and take care of the work on his end, which is to keep fighting, regardless of noise — and there’s a lot of it that he has to deal with. He does a hell of a job.”

On repeatedly rewatching Game 4 of the NBA Finals throughout the summer:

“It obviously made it 10 times better that I was a part of it. But that was my favorite game watching as a fan.”

On not considering himself a small guard and earning Brown’s defensive trust:

“(I) don’t play like that. I think Mike believes in me defensively and understands that I can definitely play a bigger point guard role.”

On the Knicks’ mutual trust despite competition for playing time:

“Yeah, I mean we just trust everybody on the roster. You never know when your number is going to be called, so we just got to be ready. And we’re big on that, you know, just trust each other, and whoever is out there, we believe they’re going to win the game.

“I mean, it showed from last year. If you look at how we celebrated when we were winning and you know certain people, certain roles, were doing what they were supposed to do and we just had to cheer them on — genuinely. We really care about each other, and we know whoever’s name is out there, we’re going to just believe in whoever is out there and win the game.”
